title: IBM PC 5150: the computer that defined the PC era
custom_excerpt: Launched in 1981, the IBM PC 5150 transformed personal computing, creating the standard that shaped the entire home and corporate computer industry.
meta_title: IBM PC 5150: the computer that defined the PC era | Ecobraz
meta_description: Launched in 1981, the IBM PC 5150 transformed personal computing and created the open standard that shaped the home and corporate computer industry.
html:
Launched in 1981, the IBM PC 5150 transformed personal computing, creating the standard that shaped the entire home and corporate computer industry.

The IBM PC 5150, launched on 12 August 1981, is regarded as the starting point of modern personal computing. Produced by the International Business Machines Corporation (IBM), it established the technical and commercial format that still underpins the machines known today as “PCs”. The expression “Personal Computer” took on real meaning with this equipment, which reshaped both the corporate and the home market.

  • Brand: IBM
  • Model: Personal Computer 5150
  • Type: Desktop personal computer
  • Origin: United States
  • Year of launch: 1981
  • Category: Computing equipment

At the turn of the 1980s, IBM was a global reference in corporate computers, but the home market was on the rise. Companies such as Apple, Commodore and Tandy were already exploring this segment. IBM, which traditionally operated with closed systems, decided to create a product that was affordable, modular and compatible with off-the-shelf components. The result was the IBM 5150, the first computer with an open architecture and a design that could be replicated by other manufacturers.

To accelerate the project, IBM set up an independent team called the “Entry Systems Division”, led by Don Estridge. In just 12 months, the team developed the system using parts available on the market and the MS-DOS operating system, licensed from Microsoft. This model of rapid, open development revolutionised the industry and gave rise to the ecosystem of compatible computers known as “IBM PC Compatible”.

The IBM PC 5150 featured a functional, robust design, typical of the professional equipment of the period. The rectangular beige case housed the dual 5¼-inch floppy disk unit, expansion slots and a motherboard with a socket for the processor. The green or amber monochrome monitor, the 83-key mechanical keyboard and the thick cables reflected the technical aesthetic of the 1980s.

Despite its simple appearance, the 5150 was designed to be versatile. Its serial and parallel ports allowed printers, modems and external peripherals to be connected, while the floppy-based operating system made it easy to start up and swap programs. This modular concept would be carried through into every PC over the decades that followed.

  • Processor: Intel 8088 (4.77 MHz, 16-bit internal / 8-bit external)
  • RAM: 16 KB to 256 KB (expandable)
  • Storage: 1 or 2 floppy disk drives, 5¼" (160–360 KB each)
  • Video card: MDA (text) or CGA (basic colours)
  • Operating system: PC-DOS 1.0 (licensed from Microsoft)
  • Monitor: monochrome or colour CRT
  • Keyboard: 83 mechanical keys
  • Power: 63.5 W / 115 V
  • Weight: 11.3 kg

The great innovation of the IBM PC 5150 was the adoption of an open architecture. Instead of manufacturing every component in-house, IBM chose to use parts from external suppliers, such as Intel (the 8088 CPU) and Microsoft (the operating system). This decision allowed other companies to create compatible copies — the so-called “PC clones”.

This open ecosystem turned personal computing into a standardised global market. Manufacturers such as Compaq, Dell and HP emerged on the basis of this model, helping to make computers more widely accessible. The term “IBM Compatible” became a byword for reliability and technical compatibility.

The IBM 5150 established personal computing as a tool for work and study. Within a few years, millions of units had been sold, and the computer became a common presence in businesses, schools and homes. It drove the emergence of productivity software, such as Lotus 1-2-3, along with accounting and administrative systems.

Culturally, the IBM PC became a symbol of the information age. Its design and its text-based interface shaped the aesthetic of computing in the 1980s and 1990s. The prompt “C:\>” came to represent the start of the interactive digital era — an icon of the birth of a language between humans and machines.

From a technical standpoint, the IBM PC 5150 established the compatibility standard that still dominates the industry. Elements such as the ISA bus, the BIOS and the case format were replicated for decades. Even modern computers still preserve this technical lineage, with an architecture derived from the original model.

The success of the 5150 gave IBM command of the market until the late 1980s. However, the openness of its architecture also allowed competitors to thrive — ironically leading IBM itself to lose control of the standard it had created. This phenomenon cemented the concept of the “open platform” as an engine of technological innovation.

The body of the IBM 5150 is made of galvanised steel, ABS plastics and electronic components based on copper and lead. The CRT monitor contains phosphor and leaded glass, which requires specialist disposal. The printed circuit boards hold valuable metals such as gold and palladium, recoverable through industrial recycling processes.

Equipment of this era, when discarded incorrectly, can release toxic substances. For this reason, environmentally sound disposal is essential. Ecobraz provides collection and dismantling services for old electronic equipment, supporting the recovery of materials and helping to prevent contamination of soil and water.

Today, the IBM PC 5150 is considered a historic piece. Models in good condition may be worth between US$2,000 and US$10,000 at international auctions. Original units that still work are exhibited in technology museums such as the Computer History Museum (USA) and the Deutsches Technikmuseum (Germany). For collectors and educators, the PC 5150 represents the origin of modern computing.

More than a product, the IBM 5150 was a lesson in engineering and strategy. It proved that open standards and interoperability are keys to technological progress. Its legacy continues in universities, in engineering, computer science and hardware design courses, as a reference for modular, scalable design.

The IBM PC 5150 ushered in the era of the personal computer. Its open architecture, its economic impact and its historical value place it among the most important pieces of equipment in the history of technology. Preserving and recycling these devices is essential to understand the digital evolution and to reduce the environmental impact of electronic waste.

To discover other pieces that changed the world and to learn about responsible disposal, visit Ecobraz’s Virtual Museum of Electronics.

title: iPhone 5 (2012): the smartphone that slimmed the Retina era
custom_excerpt: Launched in 2012, the iPhone 5 brought a 4-inch Retina display, a lighter body and 4G, accelerating smartphone turnover and the volume of e-waste worldwide.
meta_title: iPhone 5 (2012): the smartphone that slimmed Retina | Ecobraz
meta_description: Launched in 2012, the iPhone 5 brought a 4-inch Retina display, a lighter body and 4G, accelerating smartphone turnover and the growth of mobile e-waste.
html:
Launched in 2012, the iPhone 5 brought a 4-inch Retina display, a lighter body and 4G, accelerating smartphone turnover and the volume of e-waste worldwide.

The iPhone 5, launched in 2012, marked the transition of smartphones towards taller screens, 4G connectivity and an even thinner, lighter design. With an aluminium body, glass front, 4-inch Retina display and Lightning connector, the iPhone 5 consolidated a new physical and technical standard for the line. At the same time, the rapid adoption and replacement of the iPhone 5 in short consumption cycles helped increase the global volume of mobile e-waste, making the device an important piece for understanding the relationship between innovation, obsolescence and recycling.

The iPhone 5 is a bar-format smartphone with straight lines, metal edges and reduced thickness. The front is taken up by a 4-inch Retina display in 16:9 format, with a resolution of 1136 × 640 pixels and a density of 326 ppi. Above the screen sit the earpiece speaker, the front camera and the proximity and light sensors. Below, the circular physical Home button acts as the main interface control. The back combines anodised aluminium and two glass strips at the ends, housing the 8-megapixel rear camera, LED flash and microphones.

In physical terms, the iPhone 5 measures around 123.8 mm in height, 58.6 mm in width, 7.6 mm in thickness and weighs about 112 grams. The result is a device considerably lighter than its predecessor, while keeping structural robustness thanks to the aluminium unibody. The left side carries volume buttons and a silent switch; the right side holds the nano-SIM tray. At the bottom are the Lightning connector, speaker, microphone and 3.5 mm headphone jack.

The iPhone 5 was designed for continuous use as a pocket computer: calls, messaging, web browsing, email, social networks, photos, videos and a variety of applications. The combination of a Retina display, Apple A6 chip and 4G connectivity turned the iPhone 5 into a high-performance mobile terminal for the early 2010s.

By 2012, the smartphone market had already settled on the touchscreen format, but was still experimenting with different screen sizes. The iPhone 5 was the first in the line with a 4-inch display, taller than the 3.5-inch screen of previous generations. This allowed more content to be shown in lists, websites and apps, without abandoning one-handed ergonomics.

At the same time, the iPhone 5 brought support for 4G (LTE) networks in several markets. This raised expectations for browsing, streaming and app download speeds. Users began to consume more data, download larger files and stay connected on mobile networks for longer. The experience of "always-available internet" in your pocket was reinforced, and the iPhone 5 played a relevant role in that transition.

Within the iPhone family, the iPhone 5 occupies an important intermediate position. It is the successor to the iPhone 4S, keeping the design language of flat faces, metal edges and a focus on finish, while introducing three structural changes: the new Lightning connector, the increase to a 4-inch screen in 16:9 format and the adoption of a main aluminium shell.

For the Virtual Museum of Electronics, the iPhone 5 represents the start of a phase in which the hardware of the iPhone line moved closer to the aesthetics of later devices: light, thin, with heavy use of aluminium and a growing dependence on cloud services and fast networks. It is also linked to a short replacement cycle, in which many users quickly moved on to the iPhone 5s, 6 and following models, leaving a large number of iPhone 5 units sitting in drawers or sent for disposal.

As an everyday smartphone, the iPhone 5 was designed to concentrate personal and professional communication. It offers voice calls, SMS messaging, iMessage, email, messaging apps, video conferencing and access to social networks. The high-definition front camera and FaceTime support allowed good-quality video calls over Wi-Fi or 3G/4G networks.

In professional settings, the iPhone 5 can be integrated with corporate email accounts, calendars, task lists and document management applications. This turned the device into a mobility tool for professionals who relied on quick responses and remote access to work information.

The 4-inch Retina display of the iPhone 5 and the integrated GPU of the Apple A6 chip made it possible to run games, high-definition video, light photo and video editing apps, as well as music and film streaming. Users began to consume more audiovisual content directly on the device, reducing the use of dedicated devices such as music players and portable media players.

The App Store offered thousands of applications compatible with the iPhone 5, from productivity tools to complex games. This offering reinforced the role of the iPhone 5 as a software platform, not just a phone. This model, however, also contributed to accelerating obsolescence: over time, new versions of apps began to require more recent systems, leaving the iPhone 5 progressively limited.

The iPhone 5 uses the Apple A6 chip, with a dual-core CPU architecture and an integrated GPU optimised for 3D graphics and interface processing. RAM is 1 GB, a figure that, for its 2012 launch, was adequate for productivity applications, games and intensive browsing. Internal storage options include 16 GB, 32 GB and 64 GB, without a memory card slot, keeping the line's closed storage model.

This technical package allowed good fluidity on iOS 6 and subsequent updates up to the limit of official support. Over time, however, new versions of apps and systems and larger multimedia files began to strain storage capacity and memory, making the iPhone 5 less efficient for recent software.

The iPhone 5 display is a 4-inch Retina IPS LCD panel with a resolution of 1136 × 640 pixels (326 ppi). The taller aspect ratio, compared with previous generations, improves the viewing of lists, browsers and reading apps. The panel is coated with glass with an oleophobic treatment to reduce fingerprints.

The rear camera of the iPhone 5 is an 8-megapixel iSight unit with autofocus, LED flash and 1080p video recording. The front camera captures 1.2-megapixel photos and 720p video, suitable for video calls. For connectivity, the iPhone 5 includes support for 2G, 3G and 4G LTE networks (on compatible variants), dual-band Wi-Fi 802.11 a/b/g/n, Bluetooth 4.0, assisted GPS and GLONASS.

The iPhone 5 battery is an integrated lithium-ion cell, with a capacity of around 1440 mAh. It is charged via the Lightning port and cannot be removed by the user without dismantling the device. In typical use at the time, the battery lasted a day of mixed use, with calls, browsing, apps and some media consumption.

The iPhone 5 launched with iOS 6 and received updates up to later versions of the system, within Apple's support cycle. From a certain point on, the evolution of the system, combined with growing app demands, made the iPhone 5 less suited to heavy tasks. This led many users to replace it early, generating a large number of devices that were still working but considered obsolete.

The main structure of the iPhone 5 is formed by a block of machined aluminium, which acts as the chassis and rear shell. Aluminium is light, strong and recyclable, but requires industrial treatment and smelting processes for reuse. The glass strips at the rear ends and the reinforced glass front complete the protection of the screen and internal modules.

Besides aluminium and glass, the iPhone 5 incorporates engineering plastics in connectors, internal supports and guides. The combination of premium materials with plastic parts brings aesthetic and structural benefits, but increases the complexity of dismantling and sorting during recycling.

Inside, the iPhone 5 concentrates most of the electronics on a compact logic board. This board contains the A6 chip, memory, radio modules, power controllers, sensors and interfaces. It is manufactured on a laminated substrate with multiple copper layers and metal-alloy solder, along with BGA packages and high-density SMD components.

The lithium-ion battery is glued to the inside of the shell, requiring specific tools and procedures for safe removal. There are also vibration motors, speakers, microphones, cameras, flexible cables and integrated antennas. Each of these elements uses its own combinations of metals and polymers, which need to be separated for proper recycling.

The iPhone 5 sold tens of millions of units around the world. Although the device has significant technical service life, its commercial cycle was relatively short due to the launch of successor models (such as the iPhone 5s and iPhone 6). This means that many iPhone 5 units were retired before severe hardware failures, simply because they could no longer keep pace with software and performance expectations.

In practice, this produced three effects: an accumulation of iPhone 5 units kept unused, resale and reuse in secondary markets and, finally, the entry of the iPhone 5 into the electronic waste stream. In countries with weak reverse logistics structures, a significant share of these devices ends up in informal scrap yards, dumps or ordinary landfills.

Improper disposal of the iPhone 5 in ordinary waste or informal scrap involves environmental and safety risks. The lithium-ion battery can leak, deform or catch fire if punctured, crushed or short-circuited. The logic board, if burned in informal processes to extract metals, releases smoke with toxic particles and compounds.

Glass and aluminium, if fragmented without control, can cause cuts and accidents among workers who handle waste without protective equipment. The set of metals and plastics present in the iPhone 5, when abandoned in inadequate landfills, contributes to progressive contamination and the waste of resources that could be recycled.

Before disposing of an iPhone 5, it is advisable to consider reuse options. Even without comfortably running more modern systems and apps, the device can be used as a music player, a reading device, a terminal for home automation, a device dedicated to children for offline use or a test unit for simplified development.

This reuse extends the time the iPhone 5 stays out of the waste stream, reducing pressure on recycling chains and the need for new devices. However, even with reuse, there comes a point when the device no longer makes functional sense. At that point, it should be treated as electronic waste.

When the iPhone 5 is no longer of use, the environmentally responsible route is structured reverse logistics. The user should back up data, remove accounts, restore the device to factory settings, remove the SIM and, if present, any additional cards. The iPhone 5 should then be sent to an electronics collection point, a take-back campaign or a specialised collection service.

In serious recycling operations, the iPhone 5 is dismantled in stages. The battery is removed and sent for specific treatment; the logic board is directed to metal refineries; the aluminium of the shell is separated for recycling; the glass is treated as specific or recyclable waste, depending on the local chain; plastics are handled according to their composition. This process requires technology, environmental controls and traceability.

In Brazil, companies, public institutions and citizens can turn to specialised systems to route the iPhone 5 and other devices safely. One structured route is to use Ecobraz's electronics collection scheduling, which organises the collection, sorting and destination of equipment such as smartphones, tablets, computers and consoles in a way aligned with legislation and good environmental practice.

The iPhone 5 deserves a place in technology collections and museums for summarising a moment of transition: the introduction of the Lightning connector, a taller 4-inch screen, intensive use of aluminium and the reinforcement of 4G as a connectivity standard. It represents the maturity of the 2010s smartphone generation, in which the concept of a "computer in your pocket" was already established, but still far from today's sizes and capabilities.

For collectors, iPhone 5 units in good condition, with original box, intact accessories and preserved operation, have historical value and may appreciate over time. Devices with typical signs of use, but structurally intact, also serve the museological purpose of showing the practical reality of equipment that circulated on a large scale.

At the Virtual Museum of Electronics, the iPhone 5 fulfils a clear educational function: explaining to the public how an apparently "ordinary" smartphone continued the transformation of mobile communication, of the internet anywhere and of media consumption on small screens. Alongside earlier and later models, it helps visualise the evolution of size, materials and performance and, at the same time, the curve of waste generation.

The presence of the iPhone 5 in the collection reinforces the message that every device sold one day becomes electronic waste. The same technology that supports work, study and entertainment has a physical impact on the planet. To reduce that impact, the path runs through responsible reuse, extending service life and, at the end of the cycle, correct disposal. Reverse logistics initiatives, such as Ecobraz's scheduling system, close the loop of the iPhone 5: from innovation and intensive use to recycling, material recovery and environmental education through the Virtual Museum of Electronics.

title: Itai-Itai: Cadmium, Water and the Agony of the Bones
custom_excerpt: Japan's tragic contamination reveals the destructive power of cadmium and sounds a critical warning about the disposal of old batteries and corporate e-waste.
meta_title: Itai-Itai: Cadmium, Water and the Agony of the Bones | Ecobraz
meta_description: How cadmium poisoning devastated Toyama, Japan, and why negligent disposal of old NiCd batteries and corporate e-waste could repeat the disaster.
html:
Japan's tragic contamination reveals the destructive power of cadmium and sounds a critical warning about the disposal of old batteries and corporate electronic waste.

By the Environmental Investigation Team | Published in Technical Dossiers on Environmental Disasters

Some environmental catastrophes are instantaneous, marked by explosions and immediate waves of destruction. Others, however, operate with a sadistic slowness, seeping into the foundations of everyday life and exacting their price in the form of prolonged human agony. In the first decades of the twentieth century, in Toyama Prefecture, Japan, a mysterious and terrifying illness began to devastate the rural communities settled along the basin of the Jinzu River. Local inhabitants called the condition simply "Itai-Itai byō", which in its literal and anguished translation means the "ouch-ouch disease" or "it hurts, it hurts".

The disease was not a viral infection or an agricultural blight, but the terminal manifestation of a mass chemical poisoning caused by the operations of the giant Mitsui Mining and Smelting Company. Over the course of decades, the company discharged industrial wastewater laden with heavy metals into the crystalline waters of the river, which were used to irrigate the rice fields and for human consumption. The lethal agent at the heart of this nightmare was not mercury or lead, but cadmium (Cd).

This investigative dossier delves into the perverse chemistry of cadmium contamination, explaining how it corrodes the human body from the inside out. More than a historical account of one of the "Four Big Pollution Diseases of Japan", this article sets out an urgent contemporary warning: cadmium did not disappear with the end of irresponsible mining in Toyama. It is widely present in the technological fabric of our organisations, hidden in the batteries and printed circuit boards of legacy equipment. The negligent disposal of electronic waste threatens to rewrite the pain of Itai-Itai in the groundwater and soils of our own cities.

Ore extraction in the mountainous region of Kamioka began long before the disaster, but it reached a massive industrial scale during the Sino-Japanese wars and the First World War, when demand for lead, copper and zinc surged. Cadmium, a silvery-white heavy metal, is frequently found in nature associated with zinc ores. It is, in essence, an unwanted by-product of zinc refining.

Mitsui Mining did not possess (or neglected) the containment and treatment systems needed to handle this highly toxic by-product. For decades, tonnes of cadmium-rich slag were washed and discharged directly into the fast-flowing waters of the Jinzu River. The hydrogeology of the region did the rest of the tragic work. The river descended from the mountains and irrigated the vast flooded plains where rice — the staple of the Japanese diet — was grown.

Cadmium has a terrifying capacity for bioaccumulation and bioconcentration. As it settled into the mud of the rice paddies, the heavy metal was actively absorbed by the roots of the rice plants, concentrating in the grains. When the local population consumed the rice and the river water, cadmium entered their bodies in small but constant doses. Because the human body has no efficient mechanism for excreting cadmium (its half-life in the human organism ranges from 10 to 30 years), the poison simply accumulated decade after decade.

The biological impact of cadmium is among the cruellest ever documented by toxicology. The World Health Organisation (WHO) and the United Nations Environment Programme classify it as a systemic toxin of extreme danger.

When cadmium accumulates in the body, the first organs to collapse are the kidneys. The metal causes irreversible renal tubular dysfunction, preventing the kidneys from reabsorbing essential proteins and minerals. This leads to a massive loss of calcium and phosphorus through the urine. But cadmium's chemical cunning goes further: because of its atomic similarity to calcium, the body frequently confuses the two elements. Attempting to compensate for the loss of calcium in the blood, the organism begins to absorb cadmium directly into the bone matrix.

The result is a condition known as osteomalacia (extreme softening of the bones) combined with severe osteoporosis. The bones of Itai-Itai victims became so fragile and porous that they broke under the very weight of the body. Medical reports from the period describe patients — the vast majority of them middle-aged and elderly women — who suffered multiple bone fractures simply from coughing, breathing deeply or trying to turn over in bed. The pain was excruciating and unrelenting, justifying the anguished name of the disease. The victims ended up bedridden, with severe skeletal deformities, dying slowly of renal failure and malnutrition as their bones literally crumbled from within.

It took Japan decades of legal battles to force Mitsui Mining to compensate the victims and to fund the removal and replacement of millions of tonnes of contaminated soil from the rice fields. Today, the direct industrial discharge of cadmium is strictly prohibited. Yet the danger posed by this heavy metal has not been eradicated; it has merely changed its form and its address.

During the second half of the twentieth century and the beginning of the twenty-first, the electronics industry became the largest global consumer of cadmium. It found its way into the heart of our infrastructure primarily through rechargeable batteries. Nickel-cadmium (NiCd) was the dominant technology in power tools, radios, emergency lighting systems and, crucially, in server backup batteries, industrial uninterruptible power supplies (UPS) and legacy medical equipment.

Beyond batteries, cadmium was widely used as a stabiliser in PVC plastics (to prevent degradation from heat and UV light in IT cabling), in the yellow and red pigments of electronic casings, and in photosensitive components and relay contacts on older circuit boards.

What happens when an organisation today decides to clear out its store of obsolete IT equipment, full of these NiCd batteries and legacy boards, dumping them into ordinary commercial waste or with urban scrap dealers?

  • The time bomb in landfills: NiCd batteries thrown into ordinary waste end up in landfills. Over time, the metal casing of the battery oxidises and ruptures. The cadmium leaks out and mixes with the acidic leachate of the landfill. This corrosive cocktail seeps into the soil and reaches the water table. From there, the dynamic of Itai-Itai repeats itself: contaminated groundwater reaches springs and peri-urban agricultural areas, introducing cadmium into the modern food chain.
  • Fire and poisonous dust: When informal scrap collectors burn electronic waste and cables to extract base metals, the cadmium contained in the stabilised plastics and small components evaporates. Inhaling the smoke and cadmium-oxide dust is lethal, causing severe chemical pneumonitis and exponentially increasing the risk of lung cancer in the communities surrounding these clandestine operations.

The tragedy of the Jinzu River proved to us that, when it comes to cadmium, nature does not dilute the poison; it concentrates it and returns it to us through the food we eat and the water we drink. The environmental persistence of cadmium demands that organisations adopt a zero-tolerance stance towards the informal disposal of their technological legacy.

Protecting our urban aquifers against a new generation of cadmium victims depends on the immediate implementation of rigorous ESG governance practices across the technology life cycle:

  1. Rigorous identification of legacy batteries: The transition to lithium-ion batteries is recent. Company warehouses still hold thousands of nickel-cadmium and lead-acid batteries in out-of-use equipment, old two-way radios and alarm systems. These assets cannot be auctioned off as generic ferrous scrap; they are chemical liabilities of the very highest hazard (Class I waste).
  2. An absolute ban on landfilling and the informal market: Sending boxes containing old peripherals, ageing PVC cables and depreciated solar panels to informal waste pickers or rubble skips is to fund directly the contamination of your own city's soil. The leaching of heavy metals does not respect the barriers of a landfill once time and acidity act on untreated waste.
  3. Specialised dismantling at reverse-manufacturing plants: Corporate responsibility is only realised when electronic waste — and batteries in particular — is handed over to specialist, environmentally licensed recyclers. At these centres of excellence, NiCd batteries are separated by hand, packed into sealed containers and sent for hydrometallurgical or pyrometallurgical processing in negative-pressure environments. The cadmium is recovered chemically in enclosed furnaces, neutralising its potential for biological harm and allowing nickel and other valuable metals to be recycled safely.

The sound of weeping in the villages of Toyama was the price humanity paid to understand the brutality of heavy metals within our bodies. Today, we cannot claim ignorance. By treating the end of life of our electronic equipment and batteries with the scientific and ethical rigour that professional recycling demands, we work to keep the soil clean, the waters safe, and to ensure that technological progress is never again built upon the pain and fragility of the human body.

This technical analysis dossier is part of the "Environmental Disasters" series from Ecobraz Informa. We study the history of chemical catastrophes to promote responsible, preventive corporate action in the present. Documented disposal and partnership with specialised recycling centres are a fundamental safeguard for protecting biodiversity and public health against the hidden dangers in electronic waste.

Why environmental licensing matters for electronics recyclers

Environmental licensing is a fundamental requirement for electronics recyclers that intend to operate lawfully and sustainably. It confirms that recycling activities are carried out in line with environmental rules, helping to prevent harm to the environment and to public health.

Essential documents and authorisations

Before contracting an electronics recycling service, it is important to verify that the recycler holds the necessary documents, such as the environmental licence issued by the competent authorities, registration with the relevant federal technical register (Cadastro Técnico Federal, CTF) held by IBAMA, and any specific authorisations for handling and disposing of electronic waste.

Assessing the recycling process

The process used for recycling should be aligned with responsible environmental practice. Check whether there are methods for proper dismantling, safe storage of hazardous components such as batteries and chips, and measures for the correct treatment of residues in order to minimise soil and water contamination.

Compliance with applicable legislation

Environmental legislation for electronic waste is demanding and is updated regularly. Confirm that the recycler operates in line with rules such as the National Solid Waste Policy (Política Nacional de Resíduos Sólidos, PNRS) and any applicable state and municipal regulations, so as to reduce legal exposure and negative environmental impact.

Environmental inspections and audits

Check whether the recycler is regularly subject to environmental inspections carried out by supervisory bodies. These assessments help to confirm that the required environmental conditions are being maintained and that any irregularities are corrected.

Post-consumer responsibility and final disposal

A decisive point is to make sure the recycler is committed to post-consumer responsibility, arranging appropriate final disposal of residues that cannot be recycled, for example by sending them to licensed landfills or to processes that support material recovery or safe disposal.

Certifications and good practice

Beyond environmental licensing, recognised certifications such as ISO 14001 indicate that an effective environmental management system is in place. It is also positive to consider whether the recycler runs environmental awareness initiatives and adopts practices that support the circular economy.

Site visit and review of equipment

A technical site visit can give greater confidence when contracting. Review the infrastructure and the equipment in use to confirm that they are modern, efficient and designed to minimise environmental impact during the recycling process.

Transparency and environmental reporting

Ask for periodic reports that document the environmental management of the recycling process. Transparent communication reinforces credibility and demonstrates a genuine commitment to the environment.

Conclusion

Before contracting an electronics recycler, carrying out a detailed review of its environmental licensing and operating practices is essential to support legal compliance and sustainability. This precaution contributes to environmental protection and to strengthening the circular economy in the electronics sector.

Introduction to Electronic Waste

The correct disposal of electronic waste is essential to environmental protection and information security. This article presents a complete list of what can and cannot be disposed of as electronic waste, grounded in current legislation and official sources.

Definition and Importance of Electronic Waste

Electronic waste covers all discarded electrical and electronic equipment, such as computers, mobile phones, televisions and printers, that no longer has any use for the owner.

Law No. 12,305/2010, which establishes the National Solid Waste Policy, sets out guidelines for the proper handling of this waste, emphasising the shared responsibility between generators and recyclers (Law 12,305/2010).

List of Equipment That Can Be Disposed Of as Electronic Waste

  • Desktop computers and laptops
  • Display monitors
  • Mobile phones and smartphones
  • Tablets
  • Televisions
  • Printers and scanners
  • Routers and modems
  • Audio and video equipment
  • Headphones and speakers
  • Chargers, USB cables and adapters

Items That Should Not Be Disposed Of as Electronic Waste

  • Organic waste
  • Clinical (hospital) waste
  • Industrial chemical products
  • Electronic components containing hazardous materials without the appropriate disposal procedures

It is important to note that improper disposal can contaminate soil and water resources, due to the presence of heavy metals and toxic substances.

Proper Treatment and Destination

According to the National Information System on Solid Waste Management (Sinir), the correct destination of electronic equipment involves selective collection, the recovery of components and recycling (sinir.gov.br).

To make disposal easier, it is advisable to use specialist services for the collection of electronic waste, available through our electronic waste collection service.

Secure Disposal of Storage Devices

Particular attention should be given to storage devices such as hard disk drives (HDDs), SSDs, USB sticks and other media, which may contain sensitive information. The physical destruction or secure sanitisation of these devices is essential to protecting data (data destruction).

Applicable Legislation

In addition to Law No. 12,305/2010, Decree No. 10,936/2022 regulates the destination of waste electrical and electronic equipment (Decree 10,936/2022).

These rules reinforce the obligation to ensure proper disposal, selective collection and environmentally sound destination.

Closing Remarks

The correct disposal of electronic waste is a commitment to both the environment and security. Drawing on current regulations and specialist services, it is possible to minimise negative environmental impacts and help protect information.

Current Overview of E-waste in Brazil

According to the National System for Information on Solid Waste Management (SINIR) and the Ministry of the Environment (sinir.gov.br), the volume of electronic waste in the country reached around 3.2 million tonnes in 2024, growing at roughly 9% a year. Applicable Legislation and Reference Standards

Under the National Solid Waste Policy (Law No. 12,305/2010), the management of electronic waste should give priority to reverse logistics, placing responsibility on those involved in the production and consumption chain to ensure environmentally sound disposal. This legislation underpins the way regional collection and treatment systems are structured.

Efficient Collection and Management of Electronic Waste

Specialised collection of electronic equipment is essential to reducing environmental impacts. Electronic components that are disposed of improperly release hazardous substances, such as heavy metals and flame retardants, contaminating soil, water and air. Outlook and Recommendations for 2025

To address this challenge, expanding separate collection, encouraging the circular economy and strengthening reverse-logistics practices are all essential. Implementing integrated policies aligned with SINIR and the National Solid Waste Policy, together with greater awareness among stakeholders, supports meaningful progress in managing electronic waste.

title: Magnavox Odyssey (1972): Discrete Electronics and Patents
custom_excerpt: A technical dossier on the Odyssey: the absence of a CPU, the passive jumper “cartridges”, the reliance on plastic overlays and the patent empire built by Ralph Baer.
meta_title: Magnavox Odyssey (1972): Discrete Electronics | Ecobraz
meta_description: A technical dossier on the Magnavox Odyssey: no CPU, passive jumper cartridges, plastic overlays, degraded batteries and Ralph Baer’s patent empire.
html:
A technical dossier on the Odyssey: the absence of a CPU, the passive jumper "cartridges", the reliance on plastic overlays and the patent empire built by Ralph Baer.

Launched in September 1972, the Magnavox Odyssey (Model 1TL200) is not merely the first home video game console; it is an artefact of the transition between analogue and digital electronics. Designed by Ralph Baer ("The Father of Video Games") at Sanders Associates and licensed to Magnavox, the Odyssey operates on engineering principles that would be unrecognisable to a modern software developer. There is no code, no "bits" in the computational sense, and no processor.

For Ecobraz, the Odyssey is ground zero for entertainment asset management. It introduced the first waste streams specific to the industry (overlay plastics, C-type batteries, RF switch boxes) and, crucially, it established the precedent that the Intellectual Property (IP) of a piece of hardware can be worth more than the hardware itself. Magnavox and Sanders Associates generated hundreds of millions of dollars in royalties and legal settlements by suing companies such as Atari, Nintendo and Activision over two decades — a vital lesson in compliance and the protection of intangible assets.

Unlike the Atari 2600 or the Fairchild Channel F that would follow years later, the Odyssey has no microprocessor (CPU). It does not "run" games; it manipulates electrical signals in real time.

  • Transistors: Approximately 40 units.
  • Diodes: Approximately 40 units.
  • Passive components: Dozens of resistors and capacitors.

The system uses a primitive form of digital logic called DTL (Diode-Transistor Logic) to generate the three "squares" on the screen: the ball, player 1 and player 2. Everything else (scoring, scenery, rules) had to be managed physically by the players, off-screen.

Impact on reverse logistics:
Recycling an Odyssey is very different from recycling a PS5. There is no BGA (Ball Grid Array) to desolder, and no complex chips from which to recover silicon. The material value lies in the copper of the tracks, in the leads of the discrete components and, marginally, in the thin gold on the card connectors. However, the historical value far exceeds any scrap value. Ecobraz's sorting identifies these items as "museum pieces", diverting them from shredding. Destroying an Odyssey today is a failure of cultural heritage management.

The Odyssey used removable printed circuit boards called "Game Cards". Visually, they look like cartridges. Technically, they are simply jumpers (switches).

The cards contain no memory (ROM) and no active circuitry. They consist only of copper tracks that connect specific pins inside the console. When you insert Card No. 1, it closes an internal circuit that tells the machine "draw a vertical line in the middle". When you insert Card No. 3, it closes another circuit that says "erase the line and show two squares".

This teaches us about the evolution of the definition of "software". On the Odyssey, the software was the physical configuration of the hardware. For Ecobraz, this simplifies disposal: there is no data security (data sanitisation) risk on the Odyssey cards. No personal data, high scores or proprietary code are stored on them. They are inert pieces of plastic and copper.

Because the Odyssey could only generate three points of light on the screen, the graphics for the games (tennis court, haunted house, roulette board) were provided by overlays: coloured transparent plastic sheets that the user attached electrostatically to the television screen.

Polymer analysis:
These sheets were made of vinyl (PVC) or acetate. After 50 years, these materials undergo degradation:

  • Exudation: PVC releases plasticisers (phthalates), becoming oily and sticky.
  • Shrinkage: The material loses dimensional stability and warps.

The disposal of these overlays is problematic. PVC is a severe contaminant in the recycling of common plastics (PET/PE). Burning PVC releases chlorinated dioxins. In collection clean-out processes, Ecobraz ensures that these materials are segregated for industrial landfill of the appropriate class or for specialised chemical recycling, avoiding cross-contamination.

The most relevant part of the Odyssey for a modern CEO is not the game, but the lawyer. Ralph Baer registered the original patent for the "Television Gaming Apparatus" (US Patent 3,728,480).

Magnavox sued Atari (over Pong), Nintendo, Mattel and Activision. Essentially, any company that wanted to make a dot move across a screen and collide with another dot had to pay royalties to Magnavox for decades.

Ecobraz lesson: This demonstrates that technical documentation and legal protection are assets every bit as tangible as the physical product. When disposing of old prototypes or engineering documents, an organisation may be throwing away evidence of priority of invention. Ecobraz offers secure destruction services, but also the cataloguing of sensitive assets before disposal, so that the client organisation's legal department is aware of what is being discarded.

The original Odyssey was designed to run on batteries. It required 6 medium-sized cells (C-type). An AC power supply was sold separately, but it was optional.

Historical environmental liability:
The batteries of the 1970s were mostly zinc-carbon, with zinc casings that degraded quickly, or the first unstable alkaline cells. Almost every Odyssey found in an attic today has severe damage to the battery contacts due to the leakage of ammonium chloride or potassium hydroxide.

Removing this corrosion ("battery acid") generates chemical waste that must be neutralised (with weak acids such as vinegar, or bases, depending on the battery type) before the plastic or metal of the chassis can be recycled. Ecobraz treats the chemical cleaning of corrosion as a mandatory pre-processing step, to prevent leached heavy metals from entering the polymer recycling chain.

The Odyssey came with a mechanical switch box that the user screwed onto the terminals of the TV aerial (VHF). This component is a mixture of plastic, steel and passive filtering components.

The RF (Radio Frequency) shielding was critical. Without it, the console turned the television into a radio transmitter, interfering with the neighbours. Recycling these boxes involves separating ferrites and brass contacts. Often, these boxes are discarded still attached to old coaxial cables, creating a tangle of copper and PVC that requires mechanical processing (shredding and density separation).

The Odyssey's casing is white and black, made of engineering plastics from the first era of mass-market consumer electronics. The white plastic tends to yellow (a process of photodegradation and oxidation of brominated flame retardants, although these were less common in 1972 than in the 1980s).

The brittleness of these "dried-out" polymers increases the risk of shattering during reverse transport. Ecobraz uses protective packaging to prevent breakage before arrival at the plant, ensuring that sorting can be carried out in a controlled manner.

The Magnavox Odyssey is physical proof that the games industry was born of pure electronic engineering and aggressive legal strategy. It did not consume software; it consumed patents and batteries.

For waste management, it represents the challenge of the "unclassifiables": it is not digital, but it is electronic; it has no memory, but it has logic. Its recycling requires the understanding that we are dealing with industrial archaeology, where preservation is often the best form of sustainability, and destructive recycling must be the last option, reserved for irreparable units.

Manage your legacy intelligently:

  • Assessment of historical collections and technical disposal: Specialist scheduling.
  • Materials science and polymer degradation: Ecobraz Reports: Science.
  • Visit where it all began: Ecobraz Museum.

title: Singer Electric Sewing Machine: the motor that clothed the world

meta_description: Launched in 1899, the electric Singer turned the home into a modern workshop and marked the dawn of domestic automation.
html:
Launched in 1899, the electric Singer turned the home into a modern workshop and marked the dawn of domestic automation.

In 1899, the introduction of the electric motor to the traditional Singer sewing machine marked a historic turning point: electricity entered the home and domestic work became mechanised. What once depended on a treadle and physical effort gained speed, precision and energy independence.

The Singer electric sewing machine represents the transition between the mechanical age and the electric age in the domestic setting. Visually, it retained the classic design with a cast-iron body, articulated arm, vertical needle and solid wooden base. Beneath the elegant structure, however, hid a small direct-current electric motor coupled to the main shaft, replacing the manually operated treadle.

The unit was powered by domestic electricity — still rare at the end of the nineteenth century — and ran at a speed up to three times faster than the treadle models. This innovation made sewing quicker, more consistent and more accessible, particularly in urban garment workshops and small family ateliers.

The Singer Manufacturing Company, founded by Isaac Merritt Singer in 1851 in the United States, was already synonymous with quality and innovation. After half a century of dominance in the mechanical market, the company launched its first electric model in 1899, adapting motors developed by the Electric Motor Corporation.

Although Singer did not invent the electric motor itself, it was a pioneer in successfully integrating it into a domestic product. This combination of electrical engineering and functional design set the standard for the modern household appliance: efficient, compact and designed for everyday use.

The purpose of the electric machine was to automate sewing, previously driven by treadle or crank. The small motor replaced physical effort, turning the shaft that moved the needle, the fabric feed and the bobbin. Speed was controlled by a foot rheostat — the ancestor of today's electric pedals.

As a result, sewing became more uniform and less tiring, allowing greater productivity in both homes and workshops. The equipment could sew thick and fine fabrics with precision, broadening its use in tailoring shops, textile industries and even hospitals and technical schools.

In the early twentieth century, the electric sewing machine became a symbol of modernity and female independence. Women who worked at home or in small garment workshops adopted the new model for its efficiency and its potential to generate income.

Fashion professionals and urban tailors also benefited from the electric motor, which significantly reduced production time. In ateliers, the continuous hum of the motor replaced the rhythm of the treadle — marking the arrival of electric work in the artisan routine.

Singer machines were manufactured with enamelled cast iron, hardened steel parts, leather belts and brass springs. The base was made of fine wood, usually oak or walnut, and served as both a carrying case and a supporting bench. The motor was composed of copper, steel and carbon in the brushes, with a ventilated metal casing.

The ornamental design, typical of Victorian aesthetics, combined precision engineering with craftsmanship. The 1899 models were the first to feature the “Singer Electric” emblem and the serial number engraved on the front plate.

Singer's electric machine had a profound impact on society. At the end of the nineteenth century, the concept of the “electric household” was still a novelty, and this equipment demonstrated the transformative potential of electrical power. The use of the motor in homes helped to popularise domestic electrification and inspired the emergence of other household appliances, such as fans and blenders.

Beyond the technological advance, the product had social value: it enabled working women to expand their financial autonomy. The equipment became a symbol of efficiency, elegance and progress, passed down from generation to generation as a prized possession.

Old sewing machine models contain heavy metals, copper, grease and electrical components that, if disposed of improperly, contaminate soil and water. The industrial paint and enamel used at the time also contained lead- and cadmium-based pigments.

For this reason, it is essential that obsolete electrical equipment be sent to specialised recycling points. Recovering copper and iron reduces environmental impact and reclaims valuable resources for modern industry.

Singer's electric machine consolidated the concept of domestic automation. Its principle of integrating mechanics and electricity paved the way for the entire household appliance industry. To this day, the electric pedal and the direct-current motor remain foundations of applied control engineering.

Original models can be seen in museums such as the Victoria and Albert Museum in London.

title: Urban Mining: The Geopolitics of Critical Minerals and Your Organisation's Strategic Role in the Circular Economy
custom_excerpt: While conventional mining devastates ecosystems to extract grams of ore, tonnes of gold, silver, copper and rare earths lie dormant in corporate IT storerooms.

html:
By Marcio Villanova, CEO of Ecobraz Emigre.

There is a statistic in the global recycling industry that tends to startle finance managers: a tonne of printed circuit boards (PCBs) from smartphones can contain up to 100 times more gold than a tonne of ore extracted from a conventional mine. Yet, despite this concentrated wealth, most organisations still treat their obsolete IT assets as "rubble" or an "operating cost".

The idea of recovering secondary raw materials from anthropogenic waste is known as Urban Mining. In a global context of resource scarcity and geopolitical instability across supply chains, your electronic scrap has ceased to be waste and become a strategic reserve of critical materials.

In this article we will unpack the economics behind recycling and how your organisation fits into that ecosystem.

1. The Periodic Table in Your Storeroom

To understand the importance of urban mining, we need to look at the chemical composition of the equipment. A server or a desktop is not just plastic and steel. It contains:

  • Precious metals: gold, silver, palladium (in contacts and processors).
  • Base metals: copper, aluminium, iron (cables and casings).
  • Rare earths and critical minerals: neodymium (in hard-drive magnets), cobalt and lithium (in batteries), indium (in LCD screens).

Extracting these materials from virgin sources is extremely costly and polluting, whereas urban mining offers an alternative with a lower carbon impact. Visit the Virtual Museum of Electronics to see how these materials have evolved historically and how component complexity has increased over recent decades.

2. The Economic Reality: Why It Is Not "Easy Money"

Here comes the corporate reality check. If there is gold in the waste, why do organisations pay for reverse logistics rather than being paid for it?

The answer lies in the cost of reverse engineering. Unlike ground mining, the "urban mine" is dispersed and complex. To recover the gold from a motherboard, you need to:

  1. Collect and transport hazardous materials safely (logistics cost).
  2. Manually dismantle heterogeneous equipment (labour cost).
  3. Separate contaminated plastic polymers (environmental cost).
  4. Process the metals chemically or thermally (industrial refining).

For most generating organisations, the intrinsic value of the material only partly covers the operational and legal-compliance costs of this entire process. So the real return for the generator (your organisation) is not directly financial (selling scrap), but rather strategic and reputational.

3. The ROI of ESG: Where the Numbers Add Up

If selling the scrap directly does not swell the cash balance, where is the value? It sits in the sustainability reporting and in risk mitigation.

Reducing Scope 3 Emissions

Organisations committed to Net Zero targets need to reduce emissions across their value chain. By sending equipment for responsible, traceable urban mining, you avoid the extraction of virgin ore, which carries an enormous carbon footprint. Recycling aluminium, for example, uses around 95% less energy than producing primary aluminium. Figures like these enter your ESG report as a positive contribution.

Supply Chain Security

Governments and major industries have already realised that depending on imports of critical minerals from conflict zones is dangerous. Fostering a domestic recycling industry helps keep strategic materials within the local production chain, reducing external dependence over the long term.

4. The Danger of "Greenwashed Recycling"

Because of the value of these metals, the informal (illegal) market is highly active. "Recyclers" operating clandestinely go only for the "prime cuts" (the copper and the gold) and dump the rest (acidic chemicals and plastics) into rivers or soil, using primitive methods such as open-air burning to extract metals.

By handing your assets to such actors, your organisation might even "make" a few pounds on the sale, but it is financing an environmental and human disaster and taking on a huge criminal liability. Serious urban mining demands traceability.

5. How to Integrate the Circular Economy into B2B Strategy

For CFOs and Directors of Sustainability, I recommend the following approach:

  • Treat disposal as an ESG investment: allocate budget for reverse logistics just as you would for financial audits. It is a compliance cost that protects brand value.
  • Require a mass balance: your recycling partner should be able to tell you, "Of the 1,000 kg we collected, 400 kg went back to the steel industry, 200 kg to the plastics industry, and so on."
  • Choose Ecobraz: our operation is designed to maximise material recovery with full legal compliance. Request an assessment of your assets here.

6. Conclusion: The Future Is Circular

There is no such thing as "throwing away". When we throw something away, we are simply moving the problem elsewhere. Urban mining is the only viable answer for a technologically dependent world with finite resources.

Your organisation has a choice: to be a repository of environmental liabilities, or to be a supplier of resources for the industry of the future. Ecobraz exists to make the second option straightforward.

Turn Your Liability into an ESG Asset

Do not leave precious and toxic metals sitting idle in your warehouse. Make sure they return to the production cycle cleanly.

Practical step: ask us about the terms for the collection and processing of corporate electronic waste. Talk to Ecobraz.

Knowledge: follow the latest sustainability trends at Ecobraz Informa.

title: Broken Monitors: Lead and Mercury Demand a Single Route

meta_description: Why CRT and LCD monitors are among the hardest e-waste to handle, and how documented collection and specialist routing keep lead and mercury out of landfill.
html:
The Logistical Nightmare: Lead, Mercury and the Risk of Contamination

The scale of electronic waste in Brazil is measured in millions of tonnes. According to data from the UN and SINIR, the country generates around 2.2 million tonnes of e-waste each year, and most of that volume never reaches the correct destination. For a collection agent, however, volume is not the only problem. Some materials, because of their inherent risk, raise the whole reverse-logistics chain to the level of an environmental emergency. Monitors and televisions, especially older cathode-ray tube (CRT) models and the first liquid-crystal display (LCD) units, embody that threat. They are a concentrate of toxicity that ordinary logistics cannot, and should not, handle.

The Logistical Nightmare: Lead, Mercury and the Risk of Contamination

As someone who deals with e-waste collection every day, I notice that monitors are often the items organisations find hardest to dispose of. The reason is simple: the scrap value they contain is negligible next to the cost of treating their hazardous components. The most dangerous e-waste is also the e-waste that is least economically viable for the ordinary cycle.

Lead in the Glass: The Toxic Legacy of CRT Monitors

Cathode-ray tube (CRT) monitors are a legacy of toxicity. The glass of the funnel and the front panel of these devices is not ordinary glass; it was manufactured with added lead (Pb). A single unit can contain up to 3 kg of lead. This heavy metal is a potent neurotoxin, especially dangerous for children and for human development.

The presence of lead in these monitors was technologically necessary to block the X-rays generated by the operation of the tube. Today, the obsolescence of these monitors has turned a technological solution into a serious environmental problem. When a CRT monitor is discarded in open dumps or ordinary landfills (which Law No. 12,305, the PNRS, prohibits), the glass breaks. The action of rain and time releases the lead, which mixes with leachate and inexorably reaches the water table, contaminating drinking water for decades.

CETESB and environmental agencies across Brazil issue continual warnings about the risk of lead. Ensuring that this material never reaches landfill is the front line of environmental protection.

Mercury: The Invisible Threat in Flat Screens (LCD)

The flat-screen (LCD) monitors that replaced CRTs brought a different but equally serious risk: mercury (Hg). Many LCD models use small backlight lamps, known as CCFLs (cold-cathode fluorescent lamps), which contain small quantities of mercury. Although the amount per unit is small, the volume of monitors discarded nationally is colossal.

Mercury is a neurotoxin that, if released into the atmosphere (through incineration or improper breakage), is easily absorbed by living organisms and accumulates in the food chain. For reverse logistics, this means that even the collection and transport of an LCD monitor must be treated as a high chemical-risk operation.

IPEA (the Institute for Applied Economic Research) and other sustainability research institutions stress that the proper management of heavy metals is the greatest environmental challenge in reverse logistics. The risk lies not in selling scrap, but in managing the toxic residue.

Containment Logistics: Ecobraz's Role in Managing the Risk

As a collection agent, our work is not simply to carry boxes. It is to manage the chain of custody and the risk. The dismantling of monitors, which requires containment rooms, negative pressure and gas-distillation technology, is not carried out at our sorting centres. That stage is the most expensive link in the chain.

The Compliant Path: Intact Transport to Processing Plants

Ecobraz acts as the risk manager working to provide a lawful and safe route for these hazardous materials:

  • Safe collection, minimal risk: we collect monitors (CRT and LCD) intact. Safety is the priority. Transporting the whole monitor minimises the risk of breakage and of lead or mercury leaking in transit.
  • Specialist routing: the material is sent directly to plants and industrial partners that hold the certifications and technology required for dismantling. Our partners are responsible for separating the leaded glass, isolating the mercury and recovering the plastic and other metals.
  • The cost is unavoidable: because of the very high complexity and cost of final treatment, which is not covered by the negligible scrap value (and may involve a charge for CRT models), our management is essential to make this stage possible. The cost is the price of environmental safety.

Governance and Compliance: The "G" in ESG

For any organisation, disposing of monitors is not a matter of choice but of compliance. The PNRS and state environmental legislation (such as CETESB's rules in Sao Paulo) require the final destination of hazardous waste to be evidenced. The risk of fines and reputational damage is considerable.

We provide the Certificate of Final Disposal (CDF), a document issued within the scope of the service that records that the high-risk residue was diverted from landfill and entered the industrial route for safe treatment. This documentation supports the environmental governance (the "G" in ESG) that Ecobraz offers.

The Action and Our Commitment

Our work is to help make the reverse logistics of e-waste complete, responsible and safe. We take on the management of that complexity to protect water resources and public health in Brazil.

The correct disposal of monitors is the clearest example that the reverse logistics of e-waste is an environmental obligation that cannot be postponed. If you or your organisation hold broken or obsolete monitors, do not put them in with ordinary waste. Do not contribute to contamination by lead and mercury.

To arrange collection of your e-waste, whether hazardous or not, contact us: contato@ecobraz.org.br.

title: Neo Geo AES (1990): Giant Cartridges and Arcade Hardware
custom_excerpt: A technical dossier on the AES: the dual-board cartridges (PROG/CHA), the pioneering Memory Card and the industrial-grade quality of its microswitch joysticks.
meta_title: Neo Geo AES (1990): Giant Cartridges & Arcade Hardware | Ecobraz
meta_description: Technical dossier on the Neo Geo AES: dual-board cartridges (PROG/CHA), the pioneering Memory Card and industrial-grade microswitch joysticks.
html:
A technical dossier on the AES: the dual-board cartridges (PROG/CHA), the pioneering Memory Card and the industrial-grade quality of its microswitch joysticks.

Launched in 1990, the Neo Geo AES broke every rule. While the competition tried to bring an experience "similar" to the arcade into the home, SNK put the actual arcade hardware inside a home console. There was no "port" or drop in quality; it was the same chip, the same code, the same game. The cost of this was astronomical, both financially for the consumer and materially for manufacturing.

For Ecobraz, the Neo Geo represents "high-end e-waste". Its components are of superior industrial quality, designed to endure in smoky arcades (the MVS version), yet housed in luxury domestic casings. Managing these assets is not about destructive recycling, but about high-value preservation, because each unit is dense in precious materials.

The Neo Geo cartridges are the largest in the history of home consoles. They are the size of a VHS tape.

Inside each cartridge there is not just one printed circuit board (PCB). There are two interconnected PCBs:

  • PROG board: Contains the program and sound data (Mask ROM chips).
  • CHA board: Contains the graphics data (sprites and textures).

Material impact: A Neo Geo game such as Metal Slug 3 holds 708 Megabits of data. This required dozens of soldered memory chips. The volume of silicon, lead solder, fibreglass and ABS plastic in a single cartridge is equivalent to 10 Super Nintendo cartridges. Recycling a batch of Neo Geo games means processing a significant amount of industrial hardware.

The Neo Geo was the first console to let a player save a game in the arcade and continue it at home, using a Memory Card.

PCMCIA/JEIDA technology:
The card followed the JEIDA 3.0 standard (the precursor to PCMCIA). Internally it used volatile SRAM memory powered by a CR2016 lithium battery.
Leakage risk: After 30 years, these batteries (often not user-replaceable without opening the card) have failed. Although coin-cell lithium leaks less than alkaline cells, leakage still damages the card's fine contacts. Ecobraz recovers these cards by cleaning the gold contacts and replacing the battery, restoring their historical function.

The AES standard controller was not a small gamepad, but a robust tabletop "arcade stick".

Industrial durability:
Unlike the "mushy" rubber controllers of the competition, SNK used real microswitches (mechanical clicks) for the directional and the buttons. These switches are made of engineering plastic, steel springs and gold/silver contacts.
They are extremely durable (millions of cycles) and easy to repair. In waste management, a broken Neo Geo controller can almost always be fixed by swapping a standard industrial switch, unlike membrane controllers that become rubbish once the rubber tears.

To guarantee arcade-perfect fidelity, the Neo Geo uses two processors working together:

  • Main: Motorola 68000 at 12 MHz (50% faster than the Mega Drive's).
  • Sound/co-processor: Zilog Z80A at 4 MHz.

This classic combination is the "gold standard" of the 1990s. The presence of a Yamaha YM2610 sound chip (FM synthesis) adds recovery value. Unrepairable Neo Geo boards are rich sources of chips for repairing pinball machines and other arcades of the same era.

Neo Geo marketing claimed "MAX 330 MEGA - PRO GEAR SPEC" and "24-Bit". Technically, it was a 16-bit system. The "24-bit" referred to the width of the GPU data bus to the graphics memory, a genuine innovation for moving giant sprites.

The Neo Geo AES casing is made of a very high-quality textured black ABS. Unlike the grey plastics that yellow, the AES black generally remains chemically and aesthetically stable.

This makes aesthetic reuse easier. A simple polish restores the original shine. However, the golden "NEO GEO" logo stamped on the top is a metallic paint that can complicate pure recycling of the polymer if the casing is shredded.

There are different revisions of the AES motherboard (PRO-POW, PRO-POW2, etc.). Some require 5V power supplies, others 9V (or 10V), and the polarity changes.

Burnout risk:
Using the wrong supply (e.g. a 9V supply on a 5V console) burns out the voltage regulator and, worse, can damage the video and sound RAM chips. When sorting batches of Neo Geo units, checking the serial number on the bottom label is crucial for pairing the correct supply and not destroying a valuable collector's item.

The Neo Geo AES proves that industrial quality carries a high initial environmental cost (a lot of material, a lot of plastic, a lot of silicon), but results in superior longevity.

For Ecobraz, recycling a Neo Geo is almost a financial sacrilege. The focus should be on maintenance, replacing capacitors and memory batteries, and preserving these "monuments of silicon" that represent the peak of the 2D era.

Premium hardware preservation services:

  • Recovery of old Memory Cards and battery replacement: Technical Laboratory.
  • Understand the recycling of multilayer PCBs and Mask ROMs: Ecobraz Reports: Science.
  • Visit SNK's luxury: Ecobraz Museum.

title: ANTT and ABNT standards for lithium battery transport
custom_excerpt: Brazil's ANTT and ABNT standards set requirements for packaging, labelling and documentation that underpin the safe transport of lithium batteries.
meta_title: ANTT and ABNT lithium battery transport standards | Ecobraz
meta_description: How Brazil's ANTT and ABNT standards frame the safe transport of lithium batteries: classification, packaging, labelling, documentation and good practice.
html:
Introduction to the standards for transporting lithium batteries

Transporting lithium batteries is an activity that demands rigorous attention to the standards in force, given the potential risk these items present. The regulations issued by the National Land Transport Agency (ANTT) and the Brazilian Association of Technical Standards (ABNT) are central to keeping the handling and transport of these devices safe.

Classification of lithium batteries under the ANTT

The ANTT treats lithium batteries as dangerous goods, classifying them under Class 9, which covers miscellaneous dangerous substances and articles. This classification matters because it determines the specific requirements for packaging, labelling and documentation during transport.

The ANTT also follows the recommendations of the international road-transport agreement known as the European Agreement concerning the International Carriage of Dangerous Goods by Road (ADR), adapting the requirements to the Brazilian context.

ANTT requirements for transporting lithium batteries

Transport must comply with specific rules, including:

  • Classification and identification: clear identification through dangerous-substance symbols and labels, ensuring that the vehicle and the operator are aware of the load being carried.
  • Suitable packaging: use of robust, short-circuit-proof packaging that prevents leaks and physical damage to the batteries.
  • Documentation: including the Chemical Product Safety Data Sheet (FISPQ) and transport documents that detail the dangerous contents.
  • Driver training: drivers must receive specific training for transporting dangerous goods, including lithium batteries.

ABNT standards relating to lithium battery transport

The ABNT sets complementary technical standards that help standardise safe transport practices. Among the relevant standards are:

  • ABNT NBR IEC 62133: addresses the safety of secondary lithium-ion batteries, covering electrical safety requirements and the risks associated with handling.
  • ABNT NBR ISO 9001: although not specific to transport, this standard guides quality management systems, which are important for safe logistics processes.
  • Handling and storage procedures: the ABNT also provides guidance on ideal storage conditions, avoiding exposure to extreme temperatures and humidity, factors that can compromise the integrity of batteries during transport.

Why compliance with the standards matters

Ensuring compliance with the ANTT and ABNT standards for transporting lithium batteries reduces the risk of incidents such as fires and explosions, and helps prevent environmental damage caused by leaks of chemical substances.

Meeting these guidelines also supports the inspection process and helps avoid the legal penalties that can apply in the event of non-compliance.

Challenges and good practice in transport

One of the biggest challenges in transporting these batteries is controlling temperature and avoiding mechanical impacts that could cause short circuits or internal damage.

Some recommended good practices include:

  • Separating batteries by type and state of charge.
  • Using suitably certified and labelled packaging.
  • Continuously monitoring environmental conditions during transport.
  • Ongoing training of operators for a rapid response in emergency situations.

Closing remarks

Transporting lithium batteries calls for rigorous compliance with the ANTT and ABNT standards, in order to protect the integrity of the loads, the safety of the people involved and the environment. Keeping up to date with legislation and technical standards is essential to follow changes in the sector and to maintain safe, efficient logistics practices.

title: ANVISA Rules and E-waste: Special Care When Disposing of Electromedical and Hospital Equipment
custom_excerpt: Disposing of electromedical and hospital equipment calls for compliance with ANVISA rules and environmental law, with attention to safe handling, data confidentiality and traceability.

html:
Introduction

The correct disposal of electromedical and hospital equipment is essential to safeguard environmental and sanitary safety, meeting the rules of Brazil's National Health Surveillance Agency (ANVISA) and the applicable legislation. Because this equipment operates in sensitive environments, it demands special care at end of life, both to prevent biological risks and to avoid the environmental impact associated with electronic waste.

ANVISA rules applicable to the disposal of electromedical equipment

ANVISA sets out clear guidance on the management and disposal of waste involving electromedical products. Under Resolution RDC No. 222/2018, equipment that has been in contact with biological agents must be treated as healthcare waste (RSS), which entails specific rules for containment, transport and final destination.

The rules also require the segregation of reusable equipment from single-use items, calling for cleaning, disinfection and, in some cases, sterilisation processes before final disposal.

Environmental legislation relating to hospital e-waste

The disposal of electromedical equipment must also comply with the National Solid Waste Policy, established by Law No. 12,305/2010, which governs the integrated management and environmentally sound handling of solid waste, including electronic waste. Waste must be routed to specialised management to avoid contamination of soil, water and air.

Specific care for the disposal of hospital equipment

Electromedical equipment contains electronic components and potentially toxic materials, such as heavy metals and flammable substances, that require careful handling. Dismantling to separate recyclable from non-recyclable materials should take place in controlled environments. To protect data, where hard drives or storage media are present, appropriate drive sanitisation is recommended to prevent any risk of confidential information being exposed.

Recommended processes for collection and reverse logistics

The collection of hospital e-waste differs from conventional waste due to its potentially contaminated and instrumental nature. Reverse logistics should be carried out by authorised providers, with clear protocols in line with the specifications of ANVISA and the National Information System on Solid Waste Management (SINIR).

To support environmental and sanitary compliance, an electronic waste collection should be scheduled with qualified organisations that document the collection and provide for appropriate treatment and traceability of the disposal.

Responsibilities and penalties

Organisations responsible for the improper handling of electromedical waste may face administrative, civil and criminal sanctions under environmental and sanitary law. Oversight is exercised by competent bodies such as ANVISA and IBAMA, reinforcing the need to comply with the rules to protect public health and the environment.

Conclusion

The disposal of electromedical and hospital equipment requires adherence to ANVISA's specific rules and to Brazilian environmental legislation, safeguarding operational safety, environmental protection and confidentiality. Sound management, including the sanitisation of storage devices and engaging qualified services for e-waste collection, is essential to reduce risks and support legal compliance.
