title: PDP-11: the minicomputer that shaped modern computing
custom_excerpt: Launched in 1970, the PDP-11 redefined minicomputers, influenced Unix and modern languages, and today is a rarity and a piece of historic industrial e-waste.
meta_title: PDP-11: the minicomputer that shaped computing | Ecobraz
meta_description: Launched in 1970, the PDP-11 redefined minicomputers, influenced Unix and modern languages, and today is a rarity and historic industrial e-waste.
html:
Launched in 1970, the PDP-11 redefined minicomputers, influenced Unix and modern languages, and today is a rarity and a piece of historic industrial e-waste.

The PDP-11, launched by Digital Equipment Corporation (DEC) in 1970, is one of the most important minicomputers in the history of computing. It marked a break from the logic of giant mainframes, offering a smaller, more affordable, more modular system that was extremely innovative in its bus, addressing and instruction-set architecture.

The PDP-11 was not merely a commercially successful product: it became the conceptual foundation for operating systems, languages and architectures that would dominate the decades that followed. Its direct impacts include:

  • the structure of Unix and its earliest implementations;
  • the inspiration behind the design of C;
  • the evolution of the RISC philosophy;
  • the training of generations of engineers and researchers at universities;
  • the technical foundation used in industrialisation, equipment control and automation.

Today, the PDP-11 is both a physical rarity and a prime example of historic industrial electronic waste that demands particular care in preservation and in environmentally sound disposal.

In the late 1960s and early 1970s, a growing gap separated two extremes:

  • giant, expensive, centralised mainframes;
  • microcomputers that were still non-existent or very limited.

DEC had already found success with the PDP-8, but the market wanted something more powerful. The PDP-11 emerged to:

  • offer a mid-range computer that was modular and expandable;
  • simplify programming with a clean, orthogonal instruction set;
  • allow dozens of industrial peripherals to be connected;
  • be used in universities and laboratories at a lower cost than traditional mainframes.

The result was a computer whose architecture deeply influenced everything that came afterwards.

The PDP-11 was officially launched in 1970 with the PDP-11/20 model. Over the years, dozens of variants appeared (11/05, 11/10, 11/34, 11/40, 11/44, 11/70 and so on), adapted for academic, industrial, medical, governmental and military use.

It quickly became the most influential minicomputer in the world. Among the factors behind this were:

  • the Unibus bus architecture (and later the Q-bus);
  • a simple, efficient and elegant instruction set;
  • models that scaled in price, memory and CPU;
  • the availability of hundreds of peripherals and expansion boards;
  • support from universities, laboratories and technical schools.

Among the most common applications of the PDP-11 were:

  • industrial and automation systems;
  • medical and hospital control;
  • scientific and laboratory research;
  • word processing and computation at universities;
  • electrical engineering and computing laboratories;
  • telecommunications systems and early networks.

The PDP-11 is inseparable from the history of Unix. The first portable and viable versions of Unix were written and refined to run on the PDP-11 at the Bell laboratories.

This led to important characteristics:

  • the philosophy of files as the basis of everything;
  • the modern directory structure;
  • the fine tuning between hardware and software;
  • the need for C as a portable and efficient language.

In short: without the PDP-11, Unix would not have taken the form we know, and without Unix there would be no Linux, BSD, Android, macOS and their modern derivatives.

As there were so many models, a typical PDP-11 configuration included:

  • CPU: 16-bit architecture;
  • Memory: between 4 KB and several megabytes (varying by model and period);
  • Storage: tape drives, RK05, RL01, RL02, RA81 disks and equivalents;
  • Display/terminal: VT52, VT100, VT220 terminals and so on;
  • Buses: Unibus or Q-bus depending on the model;
  • Operating system: Unix, RSX-11, RT-11, RSTS/E, TSX, among others.

Systems ranged from full racks to relatively compact units, depending on the application. Equipment for automation generally had custom frames.

A typical PDP-11 contained:

  • A robust metal structure (steel, aluminium, rails and front panels);
  • Multiple boards on a backplane, with high-density connectors;
  • Large industrial power supplies with hundreds of components;
  • Magnetic drives with motors, coated disks and read heads;
  • Control panels with switches and LEDs;
  • Thick cables and internal wiring harnesses;
  • Separate video terminals (dedicated CRT monitors).

This makes the PDP-11 a complex piece of equipment to recycle, because it brings together:

  • a large physical volume;
  • many high-value metals (copper, steel, aluminium);
  • old PCBs with lead solder;
  • motors, magnets and electromechanical components.

Many PDP-11 units were used in industry, hospitals and laboratories until the 1990s and 2000s. For this reason, they still turn up:

  • in abandoned warehouses;
  • in maintenance stockrooms;
  • in racks forgotten in sheds;
  • in decommissioned technical rooms;
  • in the IT collections of governments and universities.

The PDP-11 is bulky and heavy. If disposed of incorrectly, it generates:

  • a large volume of metal scrap;
  • environmental risks from old PCBs;
  • contaminating CRTs in older terminals;
  • high dismantling costs.

In the Ecobraz Virtual Electronics Museum (https://museu.ecobraz.net) the PDP-11 represents:

  • the bridge between mainframes and microcomputers;
  • the platform that shaped Unix and C;
  • the evolution of industrial minicomputers;
  • the importance of the proper disposal of heavy equipment.

Many PDP-11 units still appear in older companies, industrial sites and government bodies, often forgotten for decades. They require:

  • specialised technical relocation;
  • electronic decommissioning;
  • recycling of large volumes of metal;
  • segregation of legacy CRTs and PCBs.

Ecobraz works precisely in this kind of heavy industrial operation, with specialised collection, technical dismantling and licensed disposal, along with the issuance of all environmental documentation as applicable to the scope of the service.

To arrange disposal operations or educational projects on industrial electronic waste, simply get in touch: contato@ecobraz.org.br.

title: Why I Created the Virtual Electronics Museum: A Personal Manifesto on Memory, Technology and the Legacy We Leave for the Future
custom_excerpt: As the head of a reverse-logistics organisation, my daily work is dealing with technology at the end of its useful life, yet as an enthusiast who grew up taking radios and computers apart, I could not bear to see history erased.
meta_title: Why I Created the Virtual Electronics Museum | Ecobraz
meta_description: Marcio Villanova on why Ecobraz built a Virtual Electronics Museum: preserving the memory of technology while responsibly managing electronic waste.
html:
1. Resisting Technological Amnesia

By Marcio Villanova, CEO of Ecobraz Emigre.

Anyone who works with me at Ecobraz knows that I am obsessed with efficiency, metrics and environmental compliance. But there is a side of my journey that explains why I do what I do, and it is not found in the spreadsheets. It lives in the memories of a boy who spent his afternoons with a screwdriver in hand, opening up old radios just to see how the "magic" happened inside.

That smell of solder, of warm bakelite, of printed circuit boards... that was the smell of the future for my generation. Every capacitor, every valve, every chip represented the triumph of human ingenuity over inert matter.

Years later, having founded an organisation dedicated to electronic waste management, I came face to face with a painful paradox. To protect the environment, I had to destroy the very machines I so admired. Watching a classic 1980s computer or a rare games console head for the shredder caused me physical pain. I realised that, if we did nothing, we would be erasing the history of our own evolution.

1. Resisting Technological Amnesia

It was out of that inner conflict that the Virtual Electronics Museum was born. It is not merely a hobby; it is an act of resistance.

We live in an age of "technological amnesia". Today's children swipe their fingers across panes of glass (smartphones) that seem magical, with no idea of the physical complexity behind them. They do not see the components. Everything is shielded, sealed, disposable.

The Museum exists to say: "Look. Before this iPhone existed, there were thousands of engineers who designed valve-based calculators, magnetic-tape computers and brick mobile phones. Innovation is a ladder, and we stand at the top of it only because those rungs existed."

2. The Curatorial Process: Saving the Soul of the Machine

In Ecobraz's day-to-day operation, I instructed my team to adopt an "archaeologist's eye". Amid tonnes of corporate waste, they learned to spot the jewels. An Apple II, an IBM PC 5150, an Atari games console, a Transglobe radio.

When such items appear, they are diverted away from the destruction line. They pass through our "intensive care unit": they are cleaned, catalogued and photographed. We preserve their aesthetics, their engineering and, where possible, their functionality. In the virtual environment, they are given eternal life, accessible to any student or curious mind anywhere in the world, without taking up endless physical space.

3. Environmental Education through Nostalgia

I came to see the Museum as the most powerful environmental education tool we have. When I show a young person the amount of plastic, metal and glass needed to build a computer from 1995, and explain that this "monster" had less power than the watch on their wrist, the penny drops.

The evolution of technology reveals the frantic pace of consumption. The Museum makes us ask: "Do we really need to change our phone every year?". It uses nostalgia to plant the seed of conscious consumption. It shows that electronic waste is not rubbish; it is technology that has lost its momentary usefulness but that carries valuable materials and human stories.

4. An Invitation to Technology Leaders

I write this manifesto to invite you — CEO, CIO, Director — to look at your organisation's disposal with fresh eyes. Do not see only a "written-off fixed asset". See legacy.

If your organisation holds pieces that tell the story of your sector, do not destroy them anonymously. Donate them to our collection. Allow us to tell the story of how your organisation helped to build the digital world. Ecobraz handles the logistics, the preservation and the sharing.

Conclusion: The Past Illuminates the Future

I believe we can only innovate responsibly if we respect the path that brought us here. The Virtual Electronics Museum is my way of saying "thank you" to the pioneers of electronics and of ensuring that the future knows where it came from.

I invite you to browse our collection. Show it to your children, to your interns. And remember: technology passes, but the impact we leave on the world — whether waste or culture — remains.

Marcio Villanova is CEO of Ecobraz Emigre, curator of the Virtual Electronics Museum and a lifelong devotee of the engineering that moves the world.

title: Why electrical wires and cables should not go in general waste
custom_excerpt: Wires and cables thrown in general waste cause environmental harm, health risks and the loss of valuable metals. Correct disposal recovers copper and aluminium.

html:
Environmental impact of incorrectly discarded wires and cables

Electrical wires and cables contain materials that, when thrown in general waste, can cause serious environmental damage. The plastic insulation, metals such as copper and aluminium, and the chemical substances in their composition are all potential sources of soil, water and air pollution. Inadequate disposal contributes to the contamination of natural resources, harming both ecosystems and human health.

Public health risks

When wires and cables are discarded incorrectly, they can release toxic substances such as heavy metals and chemical additives — especially if they are burned in dumps or irregular landfills. Inhaling these pollutants is harmful to human health and can cause respiratory problems, allergies and poisoning. Direct contact with these contaminated materials can also affect workers and the local population.

Loss of valuable raw material

The copper and aluminium in wires and cables are valuable metals that can be recycled and reused. Throwing these materials in general waste is a significant waste of natural resources and energy. Recycling these metals saves energy, reduces mining and lowers the environmental impact of producing new materials.

Why recycling and correct disposal matter

There are dedicated collection points for used electrical wires and cables, where these materials are sent for proper treatment and recycling. Directing this waste correctly minimises environmental impact, recovers valuable materials and supports the circular economy. Everyone's awareness and commitment are essential to keep this waste out of general refuse.

How to dispose of wires and cables correctly

To dispose of electrical wires and cables properly, look for collection points at recycling centres, specialist shops or take-back campaigns. Some municipalities also run selective-collection programmes specifically for electronic waste. Never place these materials in ordinary household waste, to avoid the problems described above.

Conclusion

Wires and cables contain components that, if discarded improperly, can cause environmental damage and health risks. Throwing them in general waste also loses the chance to reuse valuable metals and support sustainability. Disposing of these materials correctly protects the environment and contributes to a more sustainable future. title: Why You Should Not Put Electronics in General Waste: The Real Risks
custom_excerpt: Sending electronics to general waste creates environmental, public-health and information-security risks, as toxic components contaminate soil and water.
meta_title: Why Not Put Electronics in General Waste? | Ecobraz
meta_description: Discarding electronics in general waste creates environmental, public-health and information-security risks. Understand the hazards and the responsible options.
html:
Discarding electronics in general waste creates environmental, public-health and information-security risks. Electronic equipment contains toxic substances such as lead, mercury and cadmium which, when handled inappropriately, can contaminate soil and water, directly affecting the ecosystem and human health. Irregular disposal can also lead to failures in managing waste electrical and electronic equipment in the way required by rules such as the National Solid Waste Policy (Law No. 12,305/2010).

Environmental risks of inappropriate disposal

Electronic equipment contains components with heavy metals such as lead and mercury, as well as polymers and flame retardants that do not break down easily. Disposal in general waste can release these elements into the environment, contaminating soil, groundwater and rivers. Such substances are highly hazardous and can accumulate in food chains, compromising biodiversity.

Impacts on public health

Exposure to the heavy metals and toxic substances found in incorrectly discarded electronics can have adverse effects on human health. According to the São Paulo State Environmental Company (CETESB), metals such as mercury can cause neurological problems, while cadmium is associated with kidney and bone diseases. Handling electronics outside appropriate disposal protocols increases the risks for workers and the wider population.

Legal aspects and regulatory obligations

The National Solid Waste Policy (Law No. 12,305/2010) sets out guidelines for the environmentally sound destination of waste electrical and electronic equipment and imposes responsibilities for the reverse logistics of these materials. Placing such equipment in general waste constitutes an administrative infraction that may be subject to penalties.

Information security: the importance of proper media destruction

Storage devices such as hard drives and digital media contain sensitive information which, when discarded without proper sanitisation, may be accessed by malicious third parties. Correct secure destruction of electronic data reduces the risk of information leaks and supports compliance with personal data protection legislation.

Options for appropriate disposal and collection of electronic equipment

To avoid the risks described above, responsible disposal means routing electronics to specialised collection points. Through an electronic waste collection service, organisations can arrange documented destination, supporting the safe recycling and reuse of components.

Conclusion

Discarding electronics in general waste has a negative impact on the environment, public health and information security. Observing the applicable rules and using specialised services are essential to minimising these risks and meeting the legal obligations in force in Brazil.

title: Power banks: warning signs and safe disposal
custom_excerpt: Power banks are handy, but a device that overheats, swells or smells of burning is a hazard — learn to spot the warning signs and dispose of it safely.

meta_description: Power banks can overheat, swell or smell of burning. Learn to recognise the warning signs and how to dispose of a lithium battery power bank safely.
html:
What is a power bank?

Power banks are portable devices that store energy to recharge electronics such as smartphones, tablets and other gadgets when you are away from a mains socket. They have become part of everyday life, especially for anyone who relies heavily on mobile devices.

Warning signs in power banks

Useful as they are, power banks can pose risks when they are damaged or of poor quality. It is essential to watch out for a few signs that indicate danger, such as:

  • Excessive heat: a power bank that becomes very hot during use or charging may have a damaged battery or faulty internal components.
  • Swelling or deformation: if the casing bulges, it can signal a failure in the internal circuit or the battery, creating a risk of explosion.
  • Burning smell: a strong smell of burning while the device is running is a clear sign of a problem and an immediate hazard.
  • Rapid discharge: if the power bank drains very quickly without heavy use, the battery may be faulty.
  • Charging difficulties: problems when charging or reconnecting cables point to faults in the port or the battery and should be inspected.

Precautions during use

To minimise risks, always use original or certified chargers and cables, avoid exposing the power bank to high temperatures, and do not leave the device charging for long periods without supervision.

How to dispose of a power bank safely

When a power bank reaches the end of its useful life, it is essential to dispose of it correctly to avoid harm to the environment and risks to health. Because they are classed as electrical and electronic waste and contain lithium batteries, they must not be thrown out with general waste.

Here are the steps for safe disposal:

  • Find collection points: look for drop-off points or recycling centres that specialise in electronics.
  • Do not dismantle the device: avoid opening the power bank to remove the battery, as this can be dangerous.
  • Hand it in for recycling: only hand over the complete product at appropriate locations.
  • Follow local rules: check your area's rules on electronics disposal to ensure compliance.

The impact of improper disposal

Throwing power banks out with general waste can lead to soil and water contamination because of the heavy metals and toxic chemicals they contain. Improper disposal can also cause accidents, such as fires at landfill sites.

Conclusion

Power banks are practical, essential devices, but they call for attention to warning signs and responsible disposal. Watching for signs of failure and ensuring environmentally sound disposal helps protect both your safety and the planet.

title: Standard Operating Procedure (SOP): E-Waste Collection and Disposal

Introduction to the Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) for E-Waste Collection and Disposal

A standard operating procedure (SOP) for e-waste collection and disposal is designed to support safe, environmentally responsible handling of obsolete or damaged electronic equipment. Carrying out the SOP correctly helps reduce environmental impact and address the applicable legislation, as set out in Brazil's National Solid Waste Policy (Law No. 12,305/2010).

Legislation and Official Guidance for E-Waste Handling

The handling of waste electrical and electronic equipment is regulated principally by Law No. 12,305/2010, which establishes the National Solid Waste Policy, together with Decree No. 10,936/2022. Under this legislation, improper disposal of electronic equipment can cause contamination from heavy metals and toxic substances present in the components.

It is important to follow the guidance of the National Information System on Solid Waste Management (SINIR), available at sinir.gov.br, to monitor and align with environmental standards.

Structure of the SOP for E-Waste Collection and Disposal

The SOP should cover the full path from planning, collection, temporary storage and transport through to the final destination of the electronic waste. The documentation should describe in detail the procedures for identifying, segregating and packaging equipment in line with the applicable legislation and relevant technical standards.

Procedure for Collecting Electronic Equipment

Every collection operation should involve trained personnel and suitable equipment to help preserve physical and environmental integrity. It is advisable to use an authorised third-party electronic waste collection service, which allows scheduling and supports the traceability of the waste from source to final destination.

Storage and Transport of Equipment

Collected electronic equipment should be stored in dedicated areas that are covered, isolated and adequately ventilated to help prevent environmental damage. Transport should follow the rules of CETESB and other regulatory bodies, supporting safety and traceability and helping to prevent leaks or contamination in transit.

Secure Disposal of Hard Drives and Electronic Media

The removal of sensitive data should be addressed through the sanitisation of electronic media, in line with the guidance in NIST Special Publication 800-88. For the secure disposal of hard drives, it is advisable to use specialist services for physical destruction or data-wiping procedures aligned with recognised standards, as offered under secure hard drive disposal, helping to protect an organisation's information.

Final Destination and Recycling

Electronic waste should be sent to licensed facilities for recycling or environmentally sound disposal, as set out in Decree No. 10,936/2022 and state regulations such as those of CETESB. Records of the processes and any documents issued should be kept, supporting transparency and legal compliance.

Monitoring and Ongoing Training

The effectiveness of the SOP depends on continuous training of those involved in the collection and disposal processes, as well as periodic monitoring of the practices adopted. Reviewing performance indicators supports continuous improvement and alignment with environmental legislation.

Closing Remarks

Adopting a structured SOP grounded in official legislation is essential to the responsible management of electronic waste. Following the guidelines supports legal compliance, environmental protection and the mitigation of information-security risks.

title: The Lumière Brothers' Cinematograph: the birth of cinema
custom_excerpt: Created in 1895, the Lumière Cinematograph turned still images into movement and gave rise to the modern audiovisual art form.
meta_title: Lumière Cinematograph: the birth of cinema | Ecobraz
meta_description: Created in 1895, the Lumière Cinematograph turned still images into movement and gave rise to the modern audiovisual art form. Its history and legacy.
html:
Created in 1895, the Lumière Cinematograph turned still images into movement and gave rise to the modern audiovisual art form.

The cinematograph, created by the brothers Auguste and Louis Lumière in 1895, marked the birth of cinema as both art and technology. By turning still images into movement, the invention redefined visual communication and gave rise to modern entertainment.

The Lumière Cinematograph is a cinematographic camera and projector developed in 1895 by the French brothers Auguste and Louis Lumière. Unlike earlier devices, which were only cameras or only projectors, the cinematograph combined all three functions — filming, printing and projection — in a single portable piece of equipment. This ingenious design made it the first complete cinema system.

Built from wood and metal, the cinematograph used a hand crank to move the perforated 35 mm film in front of the projection lamp. The light passed through the film and then through an objective lens, projecting the images onto a white screen. Each second of playback contained 16 frames, creating the illusion of continuous movement. The system was so efficient that it remained the technical basis of cinema for more than half a century.

The cinematograph was created in 1895 by the brothers Auguste Lumière (1862–1954) and Louis Lumière (1864–1948), sons of a photographic plate manufacturer in Lyon, France. Influenced by the experiments of Étienne-Jules Marey and Thomas Edison, the Lumières perfected the intermittent film-advance mechanism, which allowed brief pauses between frames without burning the film.

On 28 December 1895, at the Grand Café on the Boulevard des Capucines in Paris, the first paid public screening in the history of cinema took place. The event presented ten short films, among them “Workers Leaving the Lumière Factory” and “The Arrival of a Train at a Station”. Its success was immediate and worldwide, marking the official birth of the seventh art.

The cinematograph was a multifunctional machine: it recorded, printed and projected moving images. When operated as a camera, it captured the light reflected by objects onto photosensitive 35 mm film. When connected to a light source — originally an electric arc lamp — it acted as a projector, casting the images onto the screen.

This versatility made the cinematograph a revolutionary tool for photographers, scientists and artists. It turned the recording of time and space into a public spectacle, establishing the technical and aesthetic foundations of contemporary audiovisual media.

In its early years, the cinematograph was operated by hand by camera operators and projectionists trained by the Lumières themselves. The operator turned the crank to move the film and adjusted the focus and lighting. Every screening demanded technical mastery and precise control of speed — a genuine artistic craft.

Travelling screenings carried cinema all over the world. In 1896 the cinematograph reached Brazil, with screenings in Rio de Janeiro and São Paulo that delighted audiences and inaugurated the country's own filmmaking. The invention inspired experiments in documentation, journalism and fiction — transforming the way humans perceived reality.

The cinematograph was made up of a frame of carved wood and metal parts of brass and polished steel. It used optical glass lenses, precision gears and a side crank. The 35 mm film, based on cellulose nitrate, was flammable and required extreme care during projection. The electric arc lamp, positioned behind the film, produced an intense light that passed through the images to project them onto the screen.

The equipment's finish reflected the artisanal care typical of French engineering of the period. Each cinematograph was numbered and assembled by hand, with optical adjustments made individually by technicians at the Lumière company.

The Lumières' cinematograph gave rise to a new language: that of time in motion. For the first time, it was possible to record and display human actions, landscapes and events with dynamic realism. The collective experience of the screening created a new kind of art — cinema — that brought together science, industry and imagination.

Its cultural impact was immediate. The first moving images inspired artists, journalists and scientists. Cinema went on to document wars, journeys and social change, becoming one of the main tools of communication and expression of the twentieth century. The Lumières' invention gave rise not only to a new medium, but to a new way of seeing the world.

The cellulose nitrate films used in the first decades of cinema are highly flammable and toxic. Their improper disposal releases harmful gases and chemical residues into the environment. In addition, old projectors contain heavy metals and alloys with lead and copper, which can contaminate the soil.

For this reason, the treatment of obsolete cinematographic equipment requires specialised recycling. Today, museums and restoration centres follow environmental protocols for conservation and safe disposal, helping to preserve audiovisual heritage without ecological risk.

The cinematograph is the direct ancestor of all modern cameras and projectors. Its principle of intermittent capture and projection of images is still used today in digital cameras and contemporary cinema projectors. The 35 mm system created by the Lumières became the worldwide standard for more than a century.

The legacy of the Lumière brothers goes beyond the technical field: they founded a new universal language. Through light and movement, cinema came to narrate the history of humanity, uniting cultures and crossing borders. The cinematograph is therefore the starting point of global audiovisual culture.

Just as cinema preserves memories, conscious disposal preserves the future. Electronic equipment, lamps, cables and projection devices should be recycled properly. Ecobraz carries out documented collection and environmentally sound treatment of electronics, helping to prevent pollution and recover valuable materials.

Sources: Institut Lumière (Lyon), Musée des Arts et Métiers (Paris), British Film Institute, Smithsonian Institution, Ecobraz.

title: Which components of an electronic device can be recycled?
custom_excerpt: Computers, phones and televisions hide valuable materials that can be put back into use. Understand what is recyclable and how recovery works.
meta_title: Which electronic components can be recycled? | Ecobraz
meta_description: Computers, phones and televisions hide valuable materials that can be put back into use. Learn what is recyclable in electronics and how recovery works.
html:
Computers, phones and televisions hide valuable materials that can be put back into use. Understand what is recyclable and how recovery works.

Date: 16/10/2025 • Sections: Recycling, Environment, Sustainability

When we think about recycling, we usually picture paper, glass and plastic. Yet electrical and electronic equipment — such as computers, televisions, phones and printers — also holds a high potential for recovery. Each item is made up of different materials, many of them valuable and recyclable, which can be returned to industry if handled correctly.

According to the Global E-waste Monitor 2024, published by the UN and the International Telecommunication Union (ITU), the world generated more than 60 million tonnes of electronic waste in 2023. Less than 20% of that volume was formally recycled. In Brazil, the e-waste recycling rate is still below 3%, according to the Ministry of the Environment.

Electronics contain metals such as copper, aluminium, gold and silver — all of high economic and energy value. Extracting ore for new products consumes energy and generates carbon emissions. Recycling is therefore a measure of environmental and economic sustainability.

Each piece of equipment contains hundreds of different parts and materials. The recycling process consists of dismantling, separating and directing each fraction to the appropriate destination. Here are the main recyclable components:

Found in computer cases, keyboards and televisions, engineering plastics (such as ABS and polycarbonate) are shredded and turned into granules, which return to industry to make new products.

Copper, iron, aluminium, tin and zinc are present in wires, cables, structures and power supplies. After separation, they are melted down and reintroduced into industrial processes. Copper, for example, can be recycled indefinitely without loss of quality.

Circuit boards are one of the most valuable parts, as they contain precious metals such as gold, silver, palladium and copper. The recycling process is both chemical and physical: printed circuit boards are ground down and pass through controlled chemical baths to recover the metals.

Older CRT monitors and LCD or LED screens contain glass with lead, phosphor and other compounds that require specialised treatment. The uncontaminated parts are recycled and turned into new glass products.

Lithium, nickel and lead-acid batteries are recycled in controlled processes to avoid contamination. The recovered lithium, cobalt and nickel are used again by the energy and electric mobility industry.

These are made up essentially of copper and insulating plastic. In the recycling process, the copper is separated from the sheathing and re-melted, returning to the cable industry or to metal smelting. This type of material is one of the main recycling streams handled by Ecobraz.

They contain copper, iron and aluminium. After dismantling and separation, the metals are recovered and the metal casings are sent for smelting.

Resistors, capacitors and connectors contain valuable minerals in smaller quantities. These items are recycled mainly at industrial plants using mechanical separation and electrostatic separation.

  1. Receiving and sorting: the equipment arrives at the recycling centre and is classified by type and condition.
  2. Dismantling: technicians remove reusable parts and separate plastics, metals and boards.
  3. Shredding and separation: the waste is shredded and passes through magnetic and optical separators to divide the materials.
  4. Refining and purification: the metal fractions are melted or chemically treated to produce pure raw material.
  5. Return to industry: the materials go back to cable makers, smelters, manufacturers or new production lines.

Not everything can be recovered. Contaminated parts, industrial adhesives and resins that are difficult to separate are generally sent for co-processing or controlled incineration. Hazardous substances, such as lead and mercury, need specialised treatment in line with the ABNT NBR 16156 standard and CONAMA resolutions.

Ecobraz works on the collection, dismantling, separation and disposal of electronic waste across Brazil. Materials are processed in an environmentally sound manner, with documentation of final destination issued in line with the scope of each project. The organisation's work supports reverse-logistics obligations in Brazil. Find out more at ecobraz.org.

Recycling electronics is not just an environmental practice — it is a global necessity. Each piece of equipment contains dozens of valuable materials which, if discarded incorrectly, can cause contamination and a loss of resources. Proper separation and processing ensure that metals, plastics and glass return to the economy, reducing emissions and promoting sustainability. Consumers are also a fundamental part of this chain: the simple act of handing an electronic device to a licensed operator makes all the difference.

Sources: Global E-waste Monitor 2024 (UN/ITU); ABNT NBR 16156; Decree No. 10,240/2020; Ministry of the Environment; ABREE – Brazilian Association for the Recycling of Electrical and Electronic Equipment.

title: Which tax documents fit scrap dispatch versus recycling?
custom_excerpt: How to distinguish the tax documents used for dispatching scrap and recyclable material, so movements stay traceable and consistent with tax and environmental rules.
meta_title: Tax documents: scrap vs recycling dispatch | Ecobraz
meta_description: Understand which tax documents apply to dispatching scrap and recyclable material, supporting tax and environmental consistency through electronic invoices…
html:
Understanding the nature of scrap and recycling

To keep the dispatch of materials such as scrap consistent with tax rules, it is essential to understand the distinction between scrap and recyclable material. Scrap generally refers to metal residues or other discarded materials that will be reused or treated. Recycling is the process through which these materials are transformed and returned to the production cycle. Each of these situations calls for specific tax documents to support proper control and avoid legal problems.

Tax documents for dispatching scrap

When dispatching scrap, you need to issue a tax document that evidences the movement of these materials. Typically this is a scrap dispatch invoice (Nota Fiscal de Remessa para Sucata), which should contain detailed information about the type, weight and value of the scrap. It is important that the invoice makes clear that the purpose is recovery or sale. In addition, the document should observe the applicable tax legislation, such as exemptions or tax substitution rules, depending on the state and the type of material.

Tax documents for dispatching recyclable material

When materials are destined for recycling, the tax documents may vary according to the type of material and its destination. In general, a sale or recycling dispatch invoice should be issued, clearly specifying that the shipment is for industrial reuse. It is essential to record the recipient's company registration number (CNPJ) and the appropriate tax code for this type of operation. It may also be necessary to issue the Electronic Manifest of Tax Documents (MDF-e) for transporting these loads, supporting traceability.

The importance of classifying materials correctly

Correct classification of materials directly affects the type of tax document required. For example, metal scrap is taxed differently from recyclable electronic waste. For this reason, knowing the correct Mercosur Common Nomenclature (NCM) code is essential to issue tax documents that help avoid assessments and penalties. This practice also makes internal control and responses to tax audits easier.

Recommendations for tax compliance when dispatching scrap and recyclables

To keep the dispatch of scrap or recyclable materials in good order, it is advisable to:

  • keep an up-to-date register of recipients with complete tax information;
  • always issue electronic tax documents, such as the NF-e and MDF-e, for greater transparency;
  • consult the specific legislation of each state for any adjustments required;
  • retain documents for at least five years for possible checks;
  • follow the operation through to the actual destination or recycling of the materials.

Conclusion

Handling tax documents correctly when dispatching scrap and recycling material is essential to keep operations consistent with tax and environmental rules. Issuing appropriate invoices, understanding the applicable legislation and classifying materials correctly all help to avoid problems with the tax authorities and support a transparent, sustainable process.

title: Nikola Tesla's Experimental Radio: the Birth of Wireless Communication
custom_excerpt: In 1893, Nikola Tesla demonstrated the principle of transmitting power and voice through the air, paving the way for radio and all modern telecommunications.
meta_title: Nikola Tesla's Experimental Radio: Birth of Wireless | Ecobraz
meta_description: In 1893 Nikola Tesla demonstrated transmitting power and voice through the air, laying the foundations for radio and modern telecommunications.
html:
In 1893, Nikola Tesla demonstrated the principle of transmitting power and voice through the air, paving the way for radio and all modern telecommunications.

Before commercial radio, before antennas and broadcasting stations, Nikola Tesla was already dreaming of transmitting voice and energy through the air. His experiments of 1893 opened the door to the age of global communication.

Nikola Tesla's experimental radio refers to the set of devices and circuits developed by the Serbian inventor between 1891 and 1893, with the aim of demonstrating the transmission of electrical signals without the use of conducting wires. The apparatus comprised a high-frequency coil, a vertical antenna and a resonant receiver, forming the earliest wireless communication systems known in the history of electronics.

Tesla presented his experiments publicly in 1893 at the St. Louis Electrical Exhibition, describing in detail the workings of what he called the “transmission of energy and information through the air”. Decades later, the principles Tesla demonstrated would serve as the basis for the development of radio, wireless telegraphy and modern telecommunications.

The inventor was Nikola Tesla (1856–1943), one of the greatest minds in electrical engineering and a pioneer of alternating current (AC). His experiments with wireless communication began in 1891 and culminated in 1893, when he presented, in Chicago, the complete theory of an electromagnetic transmission system capable of sending signals of voice, music and energy.

In 1897, Tesla filed a series of patents describing the use of resonant coils, transmitters and tuned receivers — elements that would later be recognised as the fundamentals of broadcasting. Although Guglielmo Marconi obtained a patent for radio in 1904, the U.S. Supreme Court, in 1943, recognised that Tesla's original patents preceded and underpinned the technology.

Tesla's experimental radio was designed to demonstrate that electrical signals could be transmitted over a distance without a physical connection. It produced high-frequency electromagnetic waves using induction coils which, as they oscillated, created electric and magnetic fields able to propagate through the air. At the receiver, a coil tuned to the same frequency captured the signal and converted it back into usable electric current.

These experiments not only proved the feasibility of wireless communication but also introduced the concept of electromagnetic resonance, one of the pillars of modern electronic engineering.

Tesla's first devices were not intended for commercial use but for scientific demonstration. He used them in lectures and public exhibitions to illustrate electrical phenomena invisible to the human eye. In 1893, during the World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago, Tesla lit fluorescent lamps and drove motors at a distance, impressing engineers and scientists from around the world.

His demonstrations inspired a generation of inventors, including Marconi, Popov and Fleming, who would later develop the first systems of telegraphy and commercial broadcasting. Tesla's experimental radio was therefore more than a prototype — it was the founding concept of wireless communication.

Tesla's experimental radios were made mainly of enamelled copper coils, iron cores, glass capacitors and insulating wooden structures. The antennas used metal rods and brass spheres, responsible for emitting and capturing the electric fields.

The basis of his experiments was the Tesla coil, a high-frequency transformer capable of generating extremely high voltages. The energy produced was so intense that it created visible electrical discharges and could light lamps several metres away, without wires.

The experiments of 1893 laid the foundation of all telecommunications engineering. Tesla's idea of transmitting signals through the air led to the emergence of radio, radar, television and, later, mobile telephony and Wi-Fi. The concept of resonance and wireless transmission of energy also inspired modern projects for inductive charging and wireless power for vehicles and devices.

Beyond its technical impact, Tesla's vision shaped the way we understand global communication: a continuous system of invisible transmission linking the entire world.

The earliest radio equipment used heavy metals and chemical insulators now considered hazardous, such as lead and varnishes containing toxic solvents. The incorrect disposal of old radio components and modern electronics releases substances that contaminate soil and groundwater.

Moreover, the rapid obsolescence of electronic devices in the digital era has increased the volume of electronic waste generated. The correct treatment of this waste is essential for environmental sustainability and for the recovery of valuable metals such as copper, silver and gold present in the boards and coils.

Tesla's experimental radio is not merely an invention but a symbol of humanity's quest for universal communication. The technology he introduced provided the basis for radio, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and satellite communications. Tesla was a visionary who anticipated the concept of a worldwide data transmission network — an idea that would only take shape a century later with the internet.

Today, museums and technology institutes preserve replicas of the original experiments, highlighting their importance for science, culture and human progress.

Preserving the history of wireless communication also means protecting the environment. Old electronic equipment, antennas, wires and radios contain metals and polymers that must be recycled correctly. Ecobraz provides a system for the documented collection and responsible recycling of electronics, helping to ensure that technological progress does not become an environmental problem.

The exponential growth of electrical and electronic waste represents a global challenge. This article presents a technical ranking of the 20 countries that generate the most electronic waste, drawing on official data, and considers the importance of the safe and efficient management of these materials.

Understanding Electronic Waste

Electronic waste, or waste electrical and electronic equipment, covers discarded devices such as computers, mobile phones, televisions and other electronic equipment. The rising generation of this waste is directly linked to rapid technological change and increasing global consumption. The inadequate management of this waste affects both the environment and public health, calling for rigorous and effective regulatory approaches.

Global Ranking of the 20 Countries that Generate the Most E-waste

According to the Global E-waste Monitor 2023, a report consolidated by the UN University and official partners, the countries with the highest annual generation of electrical and electronic waste, measured in tonnes generated per year, are listed below:

This ranking reflects the quantitative volume of tonnes generated each year, mirroring each country's technological consumption and disposal practices. The official data underlines the crucial role of public policy in managing this waste.

Legislation and Regulation in Brazil

Brazil has the National Solid Waste Policy (PNRS), Law No. 12,305/2010, which sets out guidelines for the integrated and environmentally sound management of waste, including electrical and electronic equipment. The legislation establishes shared responsibility across the product life cycle, promoting correct disposal and reuse.

In addition, the technical guidance issued through SINIR sets out practices and targets for the sector, strengthening the effectiveness of the national waste management system.

Collection and Secure Disposal of Electrical and Electronic Waste

Environmentally sound collection is essential to mitigate the adverse environmental effects caused by electrical and electronic waste. To streamline this process, arranging a scheduled electronic waste collection service is recommended, ensuring appropriate logistics with documented handling.

The disposal of devices holding sensitive information, such as hard drives and digital media, requires specific security procedures for the definitive elimination of the data. Using a secure data destruction service for drives and media helps protect sensitive information during the disposal of electronic waste.

Challenges and Future Outlook

title: Data sanitisation for HDDs and SSDs: how to do it with documented assurance
custom_excerpt: Documented data sanitisation of HDDs and SSDs permanently removes information and helps prevent leaks, with methods varying by device type.
meta_title: Data sanitisation for HDDs and SSDs | Ecobraz
meta_description: How to sanitise HDDs and SSDs with documented assurance: overwriting, degaussing, ATA Secure Erase and physical destruction, aligned to recognised standards.
html:
What is data sanitisation?

Data sanitisation is an essential process for protecting the information stored on devices such as HDDs (hard disk drives) and SSDs (solid-state drives). The procedure permanently removes all data, preventing recovery and misuse.

Why documented sanitisation matters

Confirming that data has been completely removed requires methods that follow recognised protocols. Documented sanitisation provides a formal record attesting that the information was erased, which supports data-protection requirements and helps reduce the risk of leaks. Such records support the accountability obligations under the LGPD, but they are not conclusive proof before any regulator.

Differences between HDDs and SSDs in sanitisation

HDDs traditionally use magnetic techniques to write data, whereas SSDs operate through flash memory. These differences have a direct impact on the sanitisation methods used:

  • HDDs: can be handled through magnetic overwriting, encryption or physical destruction;
  • SSDs: require specific procedures because of their memory architecture and block wear, such as ATA Secure Erase commands and secure physical destruction.

Recognised methods for sanitising HDDs

Several established methods support the effective sanitisation of HDDs:

  • Multiple overwriting: filling the disk with random data several times to erase the original information;
  • Degaussing: using magnetic fields to destroy the data held on the disk;
  • Physical destruction: shredding or crushing the disk so that the data cannot be recovered.

These methods should be carried out by trained personnel to support their effectiveness and the issuing of the corresponding records.

Recognised methods for sanitising SSDs

For SSDs, the most suitable methods are:

  • ATA Secure Erase: an internal command that fully erases all data on the SSD;
  • Full encryption followed by destruction of the key: rendering the data inaccessible;
  • Physical destruction: shredding or pulverising the device to prevent recovery.

The validity of the process also depends on issuing a record documenting how the procedure was carried out.

Step by step for documented sanitisation

  1. Identify the type of device (HDD or SSD) in order to choose the appropriate method.
  2. Choose methods aligned with international standards, such as NIST 800-88, or applicable national standards.
  3. Use suitable tools and equipment to carry out the sanitisation.
  4. Request a record documenting the removal of the data.
  5. Store and manage the documentation for audits and legal compliance.

Relevant standards and regulations

Several standards address data sanitisation, notably:

  • NIST 800-88: guidance from the US National Institute of Standards and Technology on secure data disposal;
  • LGPD: Brazil's General Data Protection Law, which requires rigorous care in the handling and disposal of personal information;
  • ISO/IEC 27040: an international standard for information security and the protection of stored data.

Conclusion

Sanitising the data held on HDDs and SSDs with documented assurance is fundamental to protecting sensitive information, reducing legal risk and supporting compliance with security standards. Adopting methods suited to each type of device and securing the corresponding records are indispensable steps towards secure and responsible management of stored data.

title: Sony PlayStation 1: the CD gaming revolution
custom_excerpt: Launched in 1994, the PlayStation 1 opened the era of CD-ROM gaming and transformed digital entertainment through design, power and innovation.
meta_title: Sony PlayStation 1: the CD gaming revolution | Ecobraz
meta_description: Launched in 1994, the PlayStation 1 opened the CD-ROM gaming era and reshaped digital entertainment through design, power and innovation.
html:
Launched in 1994, the PlayStation 1 opened the era of CD-ROM gaming and transformed the digital entertainment industry through design, power and innovation.

The Sony PlayStation 1 (PS1), released officially in Japan in December 1994, is one of the most emblematic consoles in the history of technology. It was the first home console to surpass 100 million units sold worldwide, establishing Sony as a giant of electronic entertainment. More than a product, the PlayStation represented the definitive transition between the era of cartridges and the digital future of CD-ROM gaming.

  • Brand: Sony
  • Model: PlayStation (SCPH-1000 to SCPH-9000)
  • Type: Home video game console
  • Origin: Japan
  • Year of release: 1994
  • Category: Electronic entertainment equipment

In the 1990s, the video game industry was dominated by companies such as Nintendo and Sega, built around ROM cartridges. Sony, which had originally worked alongside Nintendo on a hybrid console project, decided to follow its own path after the partnership fell apart. The result was the PlayStation, a project led by engineer Ken Kutaragi, which combined cutting-edge hardware with a commercial vision focused on digital media.

While competitors were still using expensive and limited cartridges, the PlayStation adopted the CD-ROM, a format that offered up to 650 MB of storage — around 450 times more than a traditional cartridge. This shift made room for orchestrated soundtracks, real-time video and detailed 3D graphics, driving greater realism in games.

The PlayStation 1 stood out for its minimalist, symmetrical design in light grey, with the characteristic circular disc lid. The console had physical Power, Reset and Open buttons, plus front connectors for two controllers. Its original controller — the first to feature advanced ergonomics — evolved into the iconic DualShock, with vibration and analogue sensors.

The clean, industrial look of the PS1 became a symbol of the 1990s. It fitted just as well in teenagers' bedrooms as in modern living rooms, reflecting Sony's strategy of bringing the console closer to youth and adult culture at the same time.

  • CPU: 32-bit RISC (MIPS R3000A, 33.8 MHz)
  • GPU: 3D graphics processor with 1 MB VRAM
  • Main RAM: 2 MB
  • Audio: 24 stereo sound channels (44.1 kHz)
  • Media: 650 MB CD-ROM
  • Video: resolution up to 640 × 480 pixels
  • Power: 100–240 V AC, 10 W
  • Dimensions: 270 × 188 × 60 mm
  • Weight: 1.5 kg

The PlayStation was the first console to make large-scale 3D game development viable. Its open, developer-friendly architecture attracted hundreds of independent studios, creating a vibrant ecosystem. Legendary franchises such as Final Fantasy VII, Metal Gear Solid, Resident Evil and Gran Turismo were born on this system, transforming the global games market.

Sony also revolutionised video game marketing. While Nintendo focused on a younger audience, the PlayStation targeted teenagers and young adults, associating itself with electronic music, modern design and urban lifestyle. This strategy redefined the console as a cultural product rather than merely a children's toy.

The PlayStation's success was monumental. Between 1994 and 2006, more than 7,900 titles were released, together accounting for more than 960 million copies sold. The console pushed the games industry to a multi-billion scale and positioned Sony as the leading global player.

The PlayStation also helped popularise CDs as a multimedia distribution medium, influencing the design of audio equipment, DVDs and even personal computers. Culturally, it became an icon of the 1990s, representing the fusion of technology, entertainment and minimalist visual identity.

The PS1 is made up of ABS plastics, copper circuits, silicon chips and an optical CD reader. Its main environmental challenge is the incorrect disposal of metal components and the reading lens, which contains small quantities of lead and rare earth elements. In addition, the console uses power supplies with capacitors that can release toxic residues if not treated properly.

Correct recycling of this equipment is essential. Initiatives such as Ecobraz promote environmentally safe collection and dismantling, separating precious metals and reusing engineering plastics. Preserving old consoles is also a form of environmental education and a way of valuing technological history.

The PlayStation 1 has become a collector's item. Original models, especially the first Japanese SCPH-1000 series, can exceed US$1,000 at auction. Special versions, such as the PS One (the compact model released in 2000), are also highly valued. Technology and design museums, such as MoMA and the National Videogame Museum, keep original units on display.

The legacy of the PS1 is immense. It set technical and artistic standards that still influence the market. Its success paved the way for the PlayStation 2, the best-selling console in history, and for the entire line of successors (PS3, PS4, PS5). The PlayStation 1 is remembered as the turning point of the games industry — the moment when games stopped being simple entertainment and became cinematic, cultural experiences.

The Sony PlayStation 1 is a landmark in the history of consumer electronics. Combining engineering, design and innovation, it transformed global entertainment and established digital media as the standard. Its preservation is essential both for its technological relevance and for the environmental importance of raising awareness about the life cycle of electronic devices.

Learn more about the history of technology and the sustainable destiny of electronics by visiting Ecobraz's Virtual Electronics Museum.

Launched in 2000, the PlayStation 2 reshaped home entertainment, merged cinema and gaming in a single device and became the best-selling console in history.

The Sony PlayStation 2 (PS2), released in March 2000 in Japan and in October of the same year in the United States, was the console that redefined electronic entertainment. With more than 155 million units sold, the PS2 remains the best-selling video game console in history. Its combination of technical power, elegant design and an unforgettable games library turned it into a cultural and technological icon of the turn of the millennium.

  • Brand: Sony Computer Entertainment
  • Model: PlayStation 2 (SCPH-30000 and variants)
  • Type: Home video game console
  • Origin: Japan
  • Year of release: 2000
  • Category: Electronic entertainment equipment

In the 1990s, the success of the PlayStation 1 established Sony as the new leader of the video game industry. Competition with Sega and Nintendo pushed the company to develop a more powerful system, ready for advanced 3D graphics and digital media. The result was the PlayStation 2, the first console compatible with DVDs — the format that would dominate home entertainment throughout the following decade.

By combining cutting-edge technology with a competitive price, Sony turned the PS2 into a complete multimedia platform. Beyond gaming, users could watch films, listen to CDs and explore new digital experiences. This strategic positioning made the console an object of desire worldwide — both as a games machine and as the first affordable DVD player for the mass market.

The PS2 was designed by engineer Teiyu Goto, who was also responsible for the look of the PS1. The console featured minimalist vertical lines, a matte black finish and blue illumination on the “PS2” logo. Its modular structure allowed it to be used either horizontally or vertically — an aesthetic and functional innovation for the time.

The DualShock 2 controller advanced the design of its predecessor, adding analogue sensitivity to the buttons and improved vibration. The console included USB inputs, an expansion port for networking and a hard drive, plus support for 8 MB memory cards. These features made it extremely versatile, connecting to cameras, adapters and even musical peripherals.

  • CPU: “Emotion Engine” 128-bit (294 MHz, developed by Sony and Toshiba)
  • GPU: Graphics Synthesizer (147 MHz, 4 MB eDRAM)
  • RAM: 32 MB RDRAM
  • Storage: DVD-ROM (up to 8.5 GB per disc)
  • Maximum resolution: 1280×1024 pixels
  • Audio: 48 channels, Dolby Digital 5.1 (compatible)
  • Connectivity: 2 USB ports, i.Link port, Ethernet input (optional)
  • Compatibility: PS1 games and music CDs
  • Dimensions: 301×178×78 mm
  • Weight: 2.2 kg

The PS2 was not only a technical advance — it was a cultural revolution. By offering backward compatibility with PlayStation 1 games and DVD support, the console became the hub of home entertainment. By 2002 it had already surpassed 40 million units sold, driven by titles that defined generations: Gran Turismo 3, Final Fantasy X, GTA: San Andreas, God of War, Shadow of the Colossus and many others.

Sony invested heavily in marketing, turning the PS2 into a symbol of status and technology. Its longevity was remarkable: the console remained in production until 2013 — 13 years after launch. Even after two successive generations (PS3 and PS4), the PS2 continued to be used in schools, internet cafés and educational programmes, thanks to its durability and ease of maintenance.

The success of the PS2 cemented Sony’s dominance in the global market. It is estimated that the platform generated more than US$150 billion in direct and indirect revenue. It transformed the games industry into one of the leading sectors of world entertainment, overtaking cinema in business volume.

Culturally, the PS2 marked the transition of video games from a youth niche to a mainstream phenomenon. It brought generations together and influenced the visual and sonic aesthetics of the 2000s. Its soundtracks, narratives and realistic 3D graphics created new artistic languages, still studied today in game design and interactive media courses.

The body of the PS2 is made up of ABS plastics, conductive metals and silicon components. Its long life cycle significantly reduced the volume of electronic waste compared with contemporary consoles. However, the presence of lead solder and PVC-coated cables calls for controlled environmental disposal.

Specialised recycling programmes, such as those operated by Ecobraz, ensure the safe dismantling and reuse of these materials. Beyond collection, the process preserves historical parts for educational and museum purposes, turning electronic waste into instruments of sustainable learning.

Even two decades after launch, the PlayStation 2 remains highly valued. Sealed units can fetch more than US$1,000 at international auctions. Limited editions, such as the “Satin Silver” and “Ceramic White” PS2, are even more sought after. The console is also remembered for its compatibility with the EyeToy, a forerunner of motion-capture cameras.

The PS2 was the first console to transcend the toy category and establish itself as a universal multimedia platform. Its architecture influenced the development of graphics processors, digital sound systems and even rival consoles. For technology education, it represents an example of efficient design, technical longevity and balance between hardware and software.

The Sony PlayStation 2 was more than the best-selling console in history — it was the symbol of an era. It united innovation, design and culture in a single product, redefining electronic entertainment. Preserving this equipment means preserving the peak of video game engineering and a milestone of human digital creativity.

Introduction to electronic waste classification

Classifying electronic waste correctly is essential to ensure compliance with environmental rules and the proper handling of these materials, avoiding negative impact on the environment and public health.

Official standards and legislation in force

In Brazil, the classification of electronic waste is guided mainly by the National Solid Waste Policy (Law No. 12,305/2010) and complemented by CONAMA Resolution No. 401/2008, which updates the list and the criteria for hazardous and non-hazardous waste, including electronic waste.

Electronic waste classification table

ABNT NBR 10004 classifies waste into class I (hazardous), class II A (non-inert) and class II B (inert). Electronic waste is generally classified as hazardous because of the presence of heavy metals and toxic substances. Examples include:

  • Computers, monitors and CRT televisions — class I (hazardous waste);
  • Printed circuit boards — class I;
  • Equipment with an internal battery — class I;
  • Detachable metal and plastic components may fall under class II A, depending on their specific properties.

For a detailed check of the classification, consult the technical standards published by ABNT directly.

Handling and destination

Electronic waste must be handled under a Solid Waste Management Plan (PGRS) in line with the legislation in force. For an environmentally sound destination, two practices stand out:

title: The Morse telegraph: the dawn of electric messaging
custom_excerpt: Invented in 1837 by Samuel Morse, the telegraph revolutionised world communication and gave rise to the electrical transmission of information.

html:
Invented in 1837 by Samuel Morse, the telegraph revolutionised world communication and gave rise to the electrical transmission of information.

The telegraph is a device for transmitting electrical messages through coded pulses. Developed in 1837 by the American inventor Samuel Finley Breese Morse, it transformed how people communicated over long distances, marking the beginning of modern electronic communication. Its operating principle is based on sending and receiving electrical signals through conducting wires, decoded by trained operators using the famous Morse code.

The electric telegraph was created by Samuel Morse in 1837, with the support of the physicist and inventor Alfred Vail. The first public demonstration took place in 1838, and the first commercial telegraph line entered service in 1844, connecting Washington, D.C. and Baltimore in the United States.

The telegraph's main function was to transmit coded messages over long distances using electrical pulses. Each message was made up of a sequence of dots and dashes — Morse code — representing letters and numbers. This innovation cut the time to send information from days or weeks to just minutes, allowing near-instant communication between cities and countries.

Through the 19th century, the telegraph was widely used by governments, the military, newspapers and railway companies. In newsrooms, journalists relayed international news with unprecedented speed. On the railways, telegraph operators coordinated train traffic, avoiding collisions and improving efficiency. In wartime, armed forces used it to transmit strategic orders in real time.

Telegraph operators were highly specialised professionals, able to interpret and translate messages purely by the sound or rhythm of the electrical signals. Training was rigorous and demanded extreme precision, since a single error in the sequence of dots and dashes could completely change the meaning of a message.

The first telegraph models were made of wood, copper, iron and brass. The electrical circuit consisted of a direct-current battery, a conducting wire and an electromagnet that drove a needle or marker. Over the years, the equipment evolved into more robust and compact versions, incorporating polished-metal components and ceramic insulators. This combination of materials allowed greater durability and precision in the signals transmitted.

Although a historic milestone, the telegraph and its old components contain materials that are potentially harmful to the environment. Copper, the lead in old solder and metal-oxide residues can contaminate soil and groundwater if discarded improperly. Treated-wood casings can also release toxic chemical substances as they decompose.

Incorrect disposal of these historic devices or their modern replicas contributes to heavy-metal pollution, directly affecting wildlife, plant life and human health. That is why all electronic waste — even items of historical value — should be handled with environmental responsibility.

The telegraph is considered the forerunner of all modern digital communication. It paved the way for the development of the telephone, radio and, later, the internet. Beyond its technological importance, the telegraph system created the first worldwide information networks, connecting economies and societies globally.

In museums and technology collections, the telegraph is one of the most symbolic pieces of the transition from the mechanical to the electrical age. Its historical value is immense, as it represents the first time humanity controlled and used electricity to transmit knowledge and information.

Preserving the history of technology also means understanding the impact of its full life cycle. Today, millions of tonnes of electronic waste are discarded improperly every year, causing severe environmental damage. title: Colour television: the visual spectacle of the 20th century
custom_excerpt: Introduced in Brazil in 1972, colour TV combined science, engineering and art, transforming how the world saw information and entertainment.
meta_title: Colour television: the visual spectacle of the 20th century
meta_description: Introduced in Brazil in 1972, colour TV combined science, engineering and art, transforming how the world saw information and entertainment.
html:
Introduced in Brazil in 1972, colour TV combined science, engineering and art, transforming how the world saw information and entertainment.

Colour television marked one of the greatest technological and cultural revolutions of the 20th century. Its arrival not only improved the audiovisual experience but redefined the very concept of mass communication. What had been broadcast in shades of grey now vibrated in colour, shaping advertising, journalism and entertainment. The invention combined principles of physics, electronic engineering and human visual perception, opening a new chapter in the history of media.

The development of colour television began in the 1920s, when engineers such as John Logie Baird and Vladimir Zworykin experimented with mechanical and electronic image-scanning systems. But the decisive leap came in the laboratories of RCA (Radio Corporation of America) in 1950 in the United States, with the emergence of the NTSC (National Television System Committee) standard. This system used three signals — red (R), green (G) and blue (B) — encoded into a single composite video wave, compatible with existing black-and-white sets.

The optical principle is based on the additive combination of the primary colours. Each luminous pixel of the picture tube displayed a mix of these colours, producing millions of perceptible tones. The synchronisation between the video signal, the electronic scan and the coloured phosphor on the screen was a feat of technological precision. Colour television was, in essence, the first mass application of real-time image engineering.

The cathode-ray tube (CRT) was the heart of colour TV for more than four decades. Inside a vacuum glass bulb, three electron guns — one for each primary colour — fired high-speed electron beams at a phosphor layer on the screen. Metal shadow masks ensured each beam hit only its corresponding group of dots (or triad), forming the colour image line by line.

Vertical and horizontal synchronisation coordinated a full scan of the screen 60 times per second, ensuring visual stability. The magnetic-deflection circuit controlled the movement of the beams, while the video signal modulated their intensity. The result was a continuous, precise and bright image — a combination of applied physics, special materials and high-precision analogue electronics.

In Brazil, the official debut of colour television took place on 19 February 1972, during the broadcast of the Grape Festival in Caxias do Sul (RS). The country adopted the PAL-M system, a variation developed in Germany and adapted by Philips and Telefunken. This standard combined the colour stability of European PAL with the 60 Hz frequency of the American NTSC system, delivering excellent picture quality for Brazilian electrical conditions.

TV Globo and TV Bandeirantes were pioneers of the transition, investing in cameras, transmitters and colour studios. From 1974, the national production of colour televisions grew rapidly, boosting the Brazilian electronics industry. Brands such as Philco, Gradiente, CCE and Semp Toshiba consolidated the domestic market and stimulated technology consumption.

The arrival of colour TV transformed social behaviour and how people perceived the world. Variety shows, soap operas, sport and news gained an unprecedented aesthetic dimension. Football, in particular, became a visual spectacle — the green of the pitches and the colours of the flags intensified the emotion. Advertising also reinvented itself, exploring the psychology of colour to sell products and ideas.

In the 1980s, colour television established itself as the centre of the Brazilian home. “Watching TV” became a family ritual, and tube sets dominated living rooms for decades. Colour stopped being a luxury and became the standard, shaping the visual language of an entire generation.

Behind the magic of the images lay a complex electronic system. Colour televisions contained high-voltage circuits (25 kV), line transformers, power transistors and dozens of manually adjusted capacitors and resistors. Convergence adjustment — which aligned the three colour beams — was carried out with optical instruments and technical expertise. Repair workshops and electronics courses flourished across the country, training generations of specialist technicians.

Repairing CRT televisions was an exercise in precision and safety. Besides the electrical risk, the tube needed calibration and the periodic replacement of valves and transistors. This professional ecosystem sustained the technical-service industry for more than 40 years.

In the 1990s and 2000s, the arrival of LCD and plasma monitors began the decline of the CRT tube. Limited resolution and high energy consumption made the technology obsolete against flat panels. In 2007, most tube factories in Brazil and worldwide ceased operations. However, the digital transition brought new environmental challenges: millions of old televisions were discarded without proper treatment.

CRT tubes contain lead, phosphor, copper and special glass — recyclable materials, but hazardous if poorly managed. Each 29-inch tube can contain up to 3 kg of leaded glass. When discarded incorrectly, these components release toxic substances into soil and water. Safe recycling requires manual dismantling and controlled smelting, carried out at only a few specialist centres.

Television recycling initiatives in Brazil have grown since 2014, with the implementation of the National Solid Waste Policy (PNRS). Specialist companies and cooperatives dismantle old sets, separating plastics, metals and glass. The CRT tube, given its complex make-up, requires specific processes: cutting the bulb, extracting the phosphor and melting the glass in furnaces at 1,100 °C. The treated glass can be reused in ceramics or asphalt, and the recovered metals are reintroduced into the production chain.

The Ecobraz Virtual Electronics Museum values this sustainable cycle, promoting the restoration of old televisions and showing the environmental impact of technological obsolescence. Preserving emblematic sets such as the Philco Safari and the Telefunken PAL-M reinforces the importance of educating people about conscious disposal and the circular economy.

Colour TV was not just a technical innovation — it was a mirror of society. It influenced fashion, behaviour, politics and national identity. Historic broadcasts such as the 1970 World Cup, the Diretas Já movement and Halley's Comet in 1986 were followed in vivid colour by millions of Brazilians. The image stopped being mere information: it became emotion, belonging and collective record.

Even in the digital age, the fascination with the analogue aesthetic of colour TV endures. Visual artists and designers revive the effect of vibrant colours and the visual noise of CRT images as a nostalgic language and a critique of the perfection of modern screens.

Colour television symbolises the meeting of science and emotion. Its legacy goes beyond entertainment — it is a story of innovation, engineering and social transformation. From the first phosphor tube to 4K streaming, the principle remains the same: translating light into human experience. Preserving the memory of colour TV is preserving an essential part of the technological and cultural evolution of Brazil and the world.

Introduction

Disposing of old televisions correctly has become a relevant environmental and legal issue, given the make-up of their components and their potential to contaminate the environment.
